messages.body_plain:
Thanks.  I'm not sure who was writing as @mcmc_stan.

Efficiency and scalability are often conflated, but they
are usually separate concerns.  For example, if your
algorithm takes a lot of memory per data item and runs
on a single CPU, it's not going to scale no matter how
fast it is.

What often happens is that efficiency is the bottleneck
to running bigger models rather than scalablity per se.
That is, the model would fit given lots of time, just
not efficiently enough.  MCMC in general and Stan
in particular have problems with both.

Speedup and scaling comes in many forms.  We could run
on GPUs, which would definitely give us more speed, but
we might not be able to scale really well because of the
size of the derivative graph if we try to keep the entire
density expression graph in memory.

We could spend more time developing distributed
algorithms, which would let us scale out.  That's really
the only way to get true large-scale scalability.

We could also distribute with multi-threading, but that's
more likely to be an efficiency gain than a scalability gain.

Stochastic methods (like online variational inference) could
give us both speed and scalability.

We're certainly open to suggestions on what people want
implemented.  I don't think we'll be doing DIC or AIC
or BIC---we'll probably stick to the recommendations of the
LOO package.

The Rstudio people have added some neat Stan functionality.

Not sure what people want for copulas.

Discrete parameters are an issue with the modeling language.
We can't compute the Markov blanket you can compute with
a graphical model, so we can't easily compute conditionals.
We might put a graphical model wrapper layer on top of Stan,
at which point, conditionals will be possible.

- Bob

messages.subject: Cox regression beta coefficient seems not converge
messages.subject_clean: Cox regression beta coefficient seems not converge
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan users,

I am modeling a PKPD time-to-event data in a hierarchical fashion. Specifically for each subject's data there are five variables: ID (Subject ID); TIME (follow-up time); event (event indicator);  DOSE (drug dose level); PK (PK exposure). I want to use summary PK data (by DOSE level), instead of individual subject data to construct the model. Suppose there are K dose levels. Briefly speaking, the hierarchical model is:

Linear model for "PK vs. DOSE": PK_mean_k = logphi_1 + logphi_2 * log(DOSE_k) + epsilon; (k = 1, ..., K)
Cox model for "TIME/EVENT vs. PK": lambda(t | PK_mean_k) = lambda_0(t) * exp(beta * PK_k).

I followed the counting process notation for cox model as showed in this Leuk example <http://www.openbugs.net/Examples/Leuk.html>. In this example, "Y i (t) is an observed process taking the value 1 or 0 according to whether or not subject i  is observed at time t ". Since I use summary data, the different in my case is that  I count "Y i (t)" as the number of at-risk subjects at time t for dose level k. (So N i (t) counts the number of failures which have occurred up to time t at dose level k in my case.)

As a result, the parameters for the linear model part converge very well. However, the four chains of beta coefficient for Cox model don't mix well (See attached pdf file) so I am concerned with the convergence of beta. There are NO warning/exception messages about divergence at all after Stan sampling though.

My questions are: (1) for the model part, am I doing the right thing or off the track? (2) is the convergence of beta coefficient a concern? How could I improve that? (3) the "pairs" plot shows there is a perfect correlation between "logphi_1" and "logphi_2" (intercept and slope), would that be a concern?

I attached my stan model file and a plot file. Thank you very much for any comments!

Yaohui

All the bounds are inclusive.

Although you might be tempted to do something like `lower = 0.0001`, please don't. If you're getting a lot of draws on the boundary, there's something going on with the model and you should take a look. Perhaps the data is pushing the parameter up at that boundary. messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a working model for influenza for my dissertation work, using a SEIR structure based on a model initially provided by Michael Betancourt. My problem is that it's slow / doesn't converge as well as I hoped; this is partially due to complexity, but I think partially due to the structure of the model. I'm hoping people here can help me with a few specific questions, but I'm also open to basically any kind of feedback on the model! I know the model is a bit of a monster, and if anyone has ideas for how to simplify it without removing features of the model, I'd be grateful as well.

As a basic intro, I'm fitting 3 different datasets to seasonal flu. The underlying generating mechanism is the differential equation model, and the relationships to the data are a bit complex. I have the 4-compartment, 4-groups SEIR model as an ODE function, and the outputs of the number sick, etc. are used in the model block to be transformed into the actual data, based on some assumptions about the generating mechanism for the data. (Examples: Not all sick people go to the doctor, not all flulike illnesses are actually flue, not all doctors report data, and not all people who visit a doctor have lab tests done - the parameters of each of these are informed by priors.) The model fits the yearly epidemiological flu parameters, the interaction matrix, and the parameterized variables for the relationships between the data and the SEIR model.

Specific Questions:
1) Are the transformations to/from matrix form, and to/from array (both in the ODE function, and in the model section) slowing things down significantly? Is there a better way to do this?

2)  Is there a better way to fit the dataset without needing to sample both the transformed parameter vectors, and the actual inputs? (The transformations here are for structural, as opposed to sampling, reasons.)

3) Are there more vectorized ways of doing the looping I have done in the model block? Do they make a big difference?

4) Any suggestions to simplify any other parts of the model structure, without losing the current features?

Thanks for any potential help / suggestions!
David Manheim

The model, R Script for running it, and the datasets are attached.

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I'm excited to see some of these ODE models for disease in common practice but I've approached it much more
cautiously.  A colleague at UMass did some basic simulated data for the model Michael (Betancourt) coded up and
as far as we could tell the numerical performance of that simple model really depends on the parameters used
to simulate the data.  In general that's sort of a no-brainer but in this case reasonable parameter values seemed
to make the model hang or fail to converge (this wasn't exhaustive, just trying to get a handle on what needed to
be done to just be able to throw data sets at these models).  Our other main concern with doing ODE's was that
in our data sets small counts will sometimes be important and the fact that ODE-based disease models gloss over
stochasticity in transmission makes me think that there will be serious fit issues (and therefore computational issues)
unless you introduce time-varying transmission parameters.

So that's a long-winded way of asking whether you got simpler SEIR models working consistently with this type of data (or even simulated data)? Have you looked at residuals for the current fits (even if you don't feel like you have convergence it's useful to see the space the model is exploring and the in-sample predictions it generates).

I'd also be careful about the log-normal priors since they can imply a pretty big upper tail (for example, that lognormal(log(400),5) prior if you simulate a thousand draws will regularly generate values in the 10^8 range which is going to cause computational problems in an ODE model unless there is enough data to make the posterior much tighter.  In a model this complex I have no intuition so I would go with more conservative priors.

I'm sure there are ways to make the computation more efficient too but in my experience issues like lack of fit and priors allowing outlandish parameter values are the first issues to tackle.

Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
I should note that I got the SIR models fitting robustly by
setting the initial step size to a small value.  The problem
with these models is that the tails in which you tend to
explore in warmup lead to stiff systems which freeze the
Boost ODE solver.  Setting the sampler step size to a small
value initially prevents the extreme steps that can lead the
sampler into these regimes and worked pretty robustly in
my experience.

That said, we not have CVODES for truly stiff systems and
the Boost ODE solver will bail after a set number of iterations
so you shouldn’t see freezing anymore.

Priors are indeed important for these models as the nonlinearities
in the ODEs tend to induce some nasty non-identifiabilities,
especially when you’re measuring only a few components.

messages.subject: Re: (Various) Issues with efficiency of DiffEQ Model / How to simplify my stan code
messages.subject_clean: (Various) Issues with efficiency of DiffEQ Model / How to simplify my stan code
messages.body_plain:
Hi Krzysztof,

These are really good points. I do have the model converging, and I'm not finding stability problems anymore - though it took a fair amount of playing with my priors for that to occur consistently across multiple years of data.

Re: Small numbers and stability, because it is a country level model that represents a single year, with a single implied strain, I am assuming a (low) level of constant baseline infected individuals. This is a kludgy way to account for instability near low numbers, but is effective, and not dissimilar to having an initial infection level. Stochasticity in transmission is a big deal for high fidelity, but for country level models, standard, basic compartmental modeling rarely accounts for it - a known limitation. This is a reason that microsimulation and agent based models are used much more widely now. See my new publication for details! http://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR1576.html (Sorry, I'm really excited about that.)

The residuals for the model are comparable to residuals for other ODE models - not great. In this case, the big thing that reduced the systematic discrepancies was accounting for school closures - which I have rarely seen other models do, strangely. (This makes the transmission somewhat time-varying, though in a very specific way.)

Re: lognormal priors, that's a great point. I can change them, and from what I understand, it will probably help. I need a non-negative distribution, so I need to consider which of the several options that Stan now supports I want to use - any suggestions? There are now so many options in the recent versions of Stan!

Thanks for the suggestions,
David

On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 2:07:53 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:

> Hi David,
>
> I'm excited to see some of these ODE models for disease in common practice but I've approached it much more
> cautiously.  A colleague at UMass did some basic simulated data for the model Michael (Betancourt) coded up and
> as far as we could tell the numerical performance of that simple model really depends on the parameters used
> to simulate the data.  In general that's sort of a no-brainer but in this case reasonable parameter values seemed
> to make the model hang or fail to converge (this wasn't exhaustive, just trying to get a handle on what needed to
> be done to just be able to throw data sets at these models).  Our other main concern with doing ODE's was that
> in our data sets small counts will sometimes be important and the fact that ODE-based disease models gloss over
> stochasticity in transmission makes me think that there will be serious fit issues (and therefore computational issues)
> unless you introduce time-varying transmission parameters.
>
> So that's a long-winded way of asking whether you got simpler SEIR models working consistently with this type of data (or even simulated data)? Have you looked at residuals for the current fits (even if you don't feel like you have convergence it's useful to see the space the model is exploring and the in-sample predictions it generates).
>
> I'd also be careful about the log-normal priors since they can imply a pretty big upper tail (for example, that lognormal(log(400),5) prior if you simulate a thousand draws will regularly generate values in the 10^8 range which is going to cause computational problems in an ODE model unless there is enough data to make the posterior much tighter.  In a model this complex I have no intuition so I would go with more conservative priors.
>
> I'm sure there are ways to make the computation more efficient too but in my experience issues like lack of fit and priors allowing outlandish parameter values are the first issues to tackle.
>
> Krzysztof
>
> On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 11:53:36 AM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I have a working model for influenza for my dissertation work, using a SEIR structure based on a model initially provided by Michael Betancourt. My problem is that it's slow / doesn't converge as well as I hoped; this is partially due to complexity, but I think partially due to the structure of the model. I'm hoping people here can help me with a few specific questions, but I'm also open to basically any kind of feedback on the model! I know the model is a bit of a monster, and if anyone has ideas for how to simplify it without removing features of the model, I'd be grateful as well.
> >
> > As a basic intro, I'm fitting 3 different datasets to seasonal flu. The underlying generating mechanism is the differential equation model, and the relationships to the data are a bit complex. I have the 4-compartment, 4-groups SEIR model as an ODE function, and the outputs of the number sick, etc. are used in the model block to be transformed into the actual data, based on some assumptions about the generating mechanism for the data. (Examples: Not all sick people go to the doctor, not all flulike illnesses are actually flue, not all doctors report data, and not all people who visit a doctor have lab tests done - the parameters of each of these are informed by priors.) The model fits the yearly epidemiological flu parameters, the interaction matrix, and the parameterized variables for the relationships between the data and the SEIR model.
> >
> > Specific Questions:
> > 1) Are the transformations to/from matrix form, and to/from array (both in the ODE function, and in the model section) slowing things down significantly? Is there a better way to do this?
> >
> > 2)  Is there a better way to fit the dataset without needing to sample both the transformed parameter vectors, and the actual inputs? (The transformations here are for structural, as opposed to sampling, reasons.)
> >
> > 3) Are there more vectorized ways of doing the looping I have done in the model block? Do they make a big difference?
> >
> > 4) Any suggestions to simplify any other parts of the model structure, without losing the current features?
> >
> > Thanks for any potential help / suggestions!
> > David Manheim
> >
> > The model, R Script for running it, and the datasets are attached.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] parameter range
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] parameter range
messages.body_plain:
The only way to get a parameter value of 0 or 1 is
to overflow or underflow on the unconstrained scale.
Stan samples on (-inf, inf), but then maps back to
(0, 1) using inv_logit.  inv_logit will overflow or
underflow if the unconstrained value is too large or
too small (outside of (-1000, 1000) or so).

The problem comes from the Hamiltonian integrator not being able
to follow really sharp curvature using only gradient information.
So we take a step along the gradient and wind up overflowing or
underflowing.

If the model's OK and it's just a numerical problem with extreme
steps, you can mitigate the issue by reducing stepsize and
increasing adapt_delta (latter is target acceptance rate).

- Bob

>

If you're getting a lot of draws on the boundary, there's something going on with the model and you should take a look. Perhaps the data is pushing the parameter up at that boundary. If so, you might want to rethink the statistical model. If it's underflow or overflow somewhere else, then you should take care of the numerical issues.
>
> It's hard to help without seeing the actual program, so those are all guesses.

You need to put those means on the logit scale.

> aaa = c(.1, .3, .6)

And then look at softmax:

> exp(aaa) / sum(exp(aaa))
[1] 0.2583897 0.3155978 0.4260125

You can't just grab two components.  You have to solve for
the other two given that one of them's going to be fixed.

And it's also overparameterized (leading to non-identification)
with three values.  There are only two degrees of freedom
in a 3-simplex (because theta[3] = 1 - theta[1] - theta[2]).

On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 4:28:31 PM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
> Hi Krzysztof,
>
> These are really good points. I do have the model converging, and I'm not finding stability problems anymore - though it took a fair amount of playing with my priors for that to occur consistently across multiple years of data.
>
> Re: Small numbers and stability, because it is a country level model that represents a single year, with a single implied strain, I am assuming a (low) level of constant baseline infected individuals. This is a kludgy way to account for instability near low numbers, but is effective, and not dissimilar to having an initial infection level. Stochasticity in transmission is a big deal for high fidelity, but for country level models, standard, basic compartmental modeling rarely accounts for it - a known limitation. This is a reason that microsimulation and agent based models are used much more widely now. See my new publication for details! http://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR1576.html (Sorry, I'm really excited about that.)

Thanks for mentioning the report, were you involved in the dengue modeling exercise?

>
> The residuals for the model are comparable to residuals for other ODE models - not great. In this case, the big thing that reduced the systematic discrepancies was accounting for school closures - which I have rarely seen other models do, strangely. (This makes the transmission somewhat time-varying, though in a very specific way.)

Thanks for sharing your experience with this.  The systematic patterns in residuals is another feature likely to cause computational problems so it may be a place where introducing time-varying parameters would improve algorithm efficiency enough to offset the extra computational cost.  It would be great to have a plug-in component like the birthday data model for this! Seems like everyone has to re-invent the wheel for dealing with big shocks from holidays.

>
> Re: lognormal priors, that's a great point. I can change them, and from what I understand, it will probably help. I need a non-negative distribution, so I need to consider which of the several options that Stan now supports I want to use - any suggestions? There are now so many options in the recent versions of Stan!

I tend to use gamma priors (and generally spend a lot of time simulating to get the right parameters) or just do more or less standard normal priors and use a scaled logit to get them to cover the right range nicely.  Then you just need to check posterior results to make sure you're not bumping up against the upper end of the range.  There are divergent opinions on this around here so hopefully others will chime in with alternatives but in terms of taking care of computational problems the scaled logit trick works really well as long as you don't have strong background knowledge indicating that values extremely close to zero are likely.

Krzysztof

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] rstan: dropping chains
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] rstan: dropping chains
messages.body_plain:
Do you want to drop entire chains or take a subset of posterior draws? It's not easy to drop a chain from a stanfit object really, but you can easily take a sample from the array of posterior draws as you would with any array in R, or drop a chain from the array. The resulting array can still be used with shinystan (albeit with some limitations) although not with the plotting functions in RStan. However that functionality is coming soon when we standardize the plotting functionality across all of our R packages using a new and more flexible and dependency free (except for ggplot really) package. That should be ready at some point this summer.

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
I think the hierarchical shrinkage (and hierarchical shrinkage plus) priors they describe in

http://arxiv.org/abs/1508.02502

are preferable to the horseshoe. Essentially the same thing but with a t distribution with df > 1 (so shorter tail than the Cauchy) rather than the horseshoe.

When I've fit the horseshoe in the past I've also always had to set a small initial stepsize and increase adapt_delta (the target acceptance rate).

And I second Bob's recommendation to check with simulated data if you haven't already.

Jonah

> Hi all,
>
> I have a working model for influenza for my dissertation work, using a SEIR structure based on a model initially provided by Michael Betancourt. My problem is that it's slow / doesn't converge as well as I hoped; this is partially due to complexity, but I think partially due to the structure of the model. I'm hoping people here can help me with a few specific questions, but I'm also open to basically any kind of feedback on the model! I know the model is a bit of a monster, and if anyone has ideas for how to simplify it without removing features of the model, I'd be grateful as well.
>
> As a basic intro, I'm fitting 3 different datasets to seasonal flu. The underlying generating mechanism is the differential equation model, and the relationships to the data are a bit complex. I have the 4-compartment, 4-groups SEIR model as an ODE function, and the outputs of the number sick, etc. are used in the model block to be transformed into the actual data, based on some assumptions about the generating mechanism for the data. (Examples: Not all sick people go to the doctor, not all flulike illnesses are actually flue, not all doctors report data, and not all people who visit a doctor have lab tests done - the parameters of each of these are informed by priors.) The model fits the yearly epidemiological flu parameters, the interaction matrix, and the parameterized variables for the relationships between the data and the SEIR model.
>
> Specific Questions:
> 1) Are the transformations to/from matrix form, and to/from array (both in the ODE function, and in the model section) slowing things down significantly? Is there a better way to do this?
>
> 2)  Is there a better way to fit the dataset without needing to sample both the transformed parameter vectors, and the actual inputs? (The transformations here are for structural, as opposed to sampling, reasons.)
>
> 3) Are there more vectorized ways of doing the looping I have done in the model block? Do they make a big difference?
>
> 4) Any suggestions to simplify any other parts of the model structure, without losing the current features?
>
> Thanks for any potential help / suggestions!
> David Manheim
>
> The model, R Script for running it, and the datasets are attached.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Why is Stan complaining here?
messages.body_plain:
Without the transformed parameters block, this will obviously
be fine.  What's happening is that y must be getting into a
bad state at some point, then trying to pass bad derivatives
back to the dw.

You want to print the values of y as they get
created and see where things go bad (and perhaps understand
y).

I don't know anything about these models or why you're
computing a y value you don't use (though I assume this is
just a trimmed down example).

Are you sure you don't want to constrain dw > 0?

It may be an underlying problem with how derivatives are
propagated (or not) through fmax.  It's not continuously
differentiable, so we don't usually recommend using it
with parameters.

- Bob

> On Tue, Jul 12, 2016 at 1:16 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> Thanks.  I'm not sure who was writing as @mcmc_stan.
>
> Efficiency and scalability are often conflated, but they
> are usually separate concerns.  For example, if your
> algorithm takes a lot of memory per data item and runs
> on a single CPU, it's not going to scale no matter how
> fast it is.
>
> What often happens is that efficiency is the bottleneck
> to running bigger models rather than scalablity per se.
> That is, the model would fit given lots of time, just
> not efficiently enough.  MCMC in general and Stan
> in particular have problems with both.
>
> Speedup and scaling comes in many forms.  We could run
> on GPUs, which would definitely give us more speed, but
> we might not be able to scale really well because of the
> size of the derivative graph if we try to keep the entire
> density expression graph in memory.
>
> We could spend more time developing distributed
> algorithms, which would let us scale out.  That's really
> the only way to get true large-scale scalability.
>
> We could also distribute with multi-threading, but that's
> more likely to be an efficiency gain than a scalability gain.
>
> Stochastic methods (like online variational inference) could
> give us both speed and scalability.
>
> We're certainly open to suggestions on what people want
> implemented.  I don't think we'll be doing DIC or AIC
> or BIC---we'll probably stick to the recommendations of the
> LOO package.
>
> The Rstudio people have added some neat Stan functionality.
>
> Not sure what people want for copulas.
>
> Discrete parameters are an issue with the modeling language.
> We can't compute the Markov blanket you can compute with
> a graphical model, so we can't easily compute conditionals.
> We might put a graphical model wrapper layer on top of Stan,
> at which point, conditionals will be possible.
>
> - Bob

Changing to a Horseshoe+ prior and using larger degrees of freedom the divergent transitions all but disappear.

messages.body_plain:
Ah, it's the sqrt(y);  it's derivative is

  d/dy sqrt(y) = 0.5 / sqrt(y)

which is a divide by zero error at y = 0.
The more iterations of that loop you do, the more
likely it is that you'll hit that boundary.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] estimating parameters of gaussian process
messages.body_plain:
Current Stan is slow for GPs due to big autodiff expression tree for covariance matrix operations, There is work in progress to implement internal covariance function which whould provide significant speed-up. The priors and mean functions doesn't have much effect on the speed, and Linas's code is otherwise fine except it would be better to use separate l for each covariate. Half-Cauchy prior can make HMC/NUTS slower as the covariance function parameters are weakly identified and the posterior is then likely to have a thivk tail, but changing half-Cauchy to something with less thick tail is not going to make this much faster.

On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 9:31:15 PM UTC+3, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The immediate concern, however, is the discrete “arch” variable.
> Trying to model a discrete covariate like that with a GP is typically
> a bad idea.

And I think one of the great properties is of GPs is that how easy it is to build hierarchical models by using discrete covariates! I've never had problems when combining discrete and continuous covariates.  The Linas's model above already does automatically the sum of two latent GPs, that Mike proposes :)

>  Ultimately the more you cover the range of covariate
> values the better identified your GP will be (and the better it will
> fit), and with only 0 and 1 you’re not really constraining the hyperparameters
> all that much.

For a single binary covariate the covariance matrix collapses to 2x2 covariance matrix. If exponentiated quadratic (aka squared exponential) is used it has two degrees of freedoms. I think this covariance matrix would be in many cases well identified and thus also the corresponding discerete GP ie normal distribution would be well identified, although there is dependency between sigmaf and l (and sigman) making them not so well identified. What I try to say is that you don't need to worry so much about the identifiability of hyperparameters and even less in discrete case :)

Aki

Specifying a stepsize corresponds to setting an initial stepsize, and doesn't prevent it from learning the stepsize during the warmup period. Jonah

Hi,

Yes, I was involved in the Dengue modeling project, though good prediction was pretty intractable given the lack of information available; for high fidelity modeling you need lots of location, population, and geography specific data. Some cool ML approaches were tried by various teams with some success, but they require years and years of data to train, and aren't applicable to new locations or changing conditions, so there is limited policy relevance. (And the sponsors basically said they weren't hopeful that Dengue modeling could be advanced all that much.)

I have asked before about time varying inputs, and it's (appropriately) not high on the list of priorities for the core team. I'll be trying gamma priors - my first trial seems to have gotten fairly good convergence, without much fiddling, but that may be luck.

Cheers,
David

This is a kludgy way to account for instability near low numbers, but is effective, and not dissimilar to having an initial infection level. Stochasticity in transmission is a big deal for high fidelity, but for country level models, standard, basic compartmental modeling rarely accounts for it - a known limitation. This is a reason that microsimulation and agent based models are used much more widely now. See my new publication for details! http://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR1576.html (Sorry, I'm really excited about that.)

What are you trying to accomplish?  As Michael said,
if you want to drop chains that didn't converge, that
will potentially lead to biased estimates.

If you just want to subsample because there's too much
data, you want to thin existing chains rather than cut
out whole chains.  That way, the convergence diagnostics
and effective sample size estimates are reasonable.  If you
just permute, you lose all of this.

vector.

messages.body_plain:
In the degenerate 2x2 case the two parameters should be identifiable
(the variances constraining the marginal variance, the covariances
constraining the product of the marginal variance and length scale)
but they will still be nonlinearly correlated and without sufficient data
they can still be hard to fit!  At least in the world of _finite_ data.  ;-)

On Jul 13, 2016, at 7:45 PM, Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:

> For a single binary covariate the covariance matrix collapses to 2x2 covariance matrix. If exponentiated quadratic (aka squared exponential) is used it has two degrees of freedoms. I think this covariance matrix would be in many cases well identified and thus also the corresponding discerete GP ie normal distribution would be well identified, although there is dependency between sigmaf and l (and sigman) making them not so well identified. What I try to say is that you don't need to worry so much about the identifiability of hyperparameters and even less in discrete case :)
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Why is Stan complaining here?
messages.body_plain:
We've run across other examples like this recently in
fisheries population models, where there's a stepwise
approximation of what's really a diff eq with a measured
catch which can drive the population negative if it's
larger than the previously estimated size.

If you explain more about your problem, we might be able
to help at a deeper level.

Often you can get by with some kind of constraint on variables
or with turning something you think is concrete into a measured
variable.

In general, fmax() is bad news in a Stan program because
it breaks derivatives.  That is, no information flows from
the output of fmax() back to the system in cases where you
return a constant 0 and it's discontinuous in cases where
you don't when you cross the threshold.

- Bob

For the variable that is continuous but you only measured it at 2 levels, I don't believe that there's any benefit in treating it as a second continuous dimension in the GP; indeed, it may even be computationally wasteful. One of the very important features of Baysian inference is that
it decouples inference from decision making.  A natural Bayesian
fit will not feature cut-offs such as “variable included or not” but
rather try to estimate the importance of each variable.  When
you try to force decision making into an inference problem you
run into no end of trouble, as you are seeing.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Divergent transitions in meta-regression model
messages.body_plain:
Just a quick note —divergences simply indicate that Stan cannot fit the model, it does
not necessarily imply that the model is incompatible with the data (although there’s often
a strong correlation, which is the basis of the “Folk Theorem”).  But it’s important to take
divergences seriously, because if you’re not getting an accurate fit then you can’t really
judge the compatibility of your model!

Upon a very brief look your model looks appropriate — but perhaps there might be too
many random effects and what you are seeing is a consequently of extreme linear
correlations (as opposed to the nonlinear correlations that we typical worry about in
these hierarchical models).

On Jul 15, 2016, at 8:24 AM, Lauren Vollmer <vollmer...@gmail.com> wrote:

No, we're not trying to do this within Stan's samplers directly,
because it wouldn't produce the correct Bayesian posterior.

You can code up true spike-and-slab priors by marginalizing
out the is-it-zero indicator, but it requires O(2^N) amount of
work for N parameters, so it's not practical in the usual situations
for which people want to do variable selection.

Aki's been working on the problem as a post-process.  I don't know
if there's anything public other than this:

http://arxiv.org/abs/1509.04752

- Bob

To: <stan-...@googlegroups.com>

I disagree with the spike and slab idea. Instead, I think it would be better to do the add-on as I said in my earlier email. It would make sense not to do this in Stan but in R or Python. You fit the Stan model with the horseshoe prior or whatever, then you post-process and set parameters to exactly zero. This could be coded in a program in R or Python that would be a wrapper for the Stan call.

Any papers/pointers on what this would look like?  I don't mind some R programming and sharing that with the community, but I'm not sure how to adjust the remaining coefficients for the fact that one is fixed at zero during post processing.

Cheers,

Josh

We don't really have a place on the Stan webpage for this sort of wrapper or post-processing. It could be a good idea to have some of these things accessible for users. Right now we have rstanarm and loo, neither of which is part of Stan but both of which can be useful when fitting Stan models.

> On Jul 17, 2016, at 1:10 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> No, we're not trying to do this within Stan's samplers directly,
> because it wouldn't produce the correct Bayesian posterior.
>
> You can code up true spike-and-slab priors by marginalizing
> out the is-it-zero indicator, but it requires O(2^N) amount of
> work for N parameters, so it's not practical in the usual situations
> for which people want to do variable selection.
>
> Aki's been working on the problem as a post-process. I don't know
> if there's anything public other than this:
>
> http://arxiv.org/abs/1509.04752
>
> - Bob

For example, I could imagine having Stan take parameters whose posteriors are tight near zero, and then setting then to be exactly 0, and then going on from there to run with constraints. That could be worth doing, but I think it should be an explicit part of the processing, not something that gets done by the prior.

Particularly in the case of models where the predictors are of substantive interest, it would be very convenient to be able to shrink very small coefficients, say for interactions, to zero, so that the effects of the individual variables making up the interaction have a simpler interpretation. I have been playing with the horseshoe prior, but it is inconvenient to have even very small non-zero interaction terms when trying to present the major paths from a model.
>>

>>
>> Josh

>> A

messages.body_plain:
I would not adjust the remaining coefficients.  I'd just fit the model and then have some rule of reporting to zero the coefs that are lower than some threshold.
If you do want to go back and re-fit the model using the coefs set to 0, you'd need to have an alternative version of your Stan program that enters these as data.  But I don't think that's a good idea.  The whole point is that the coefs aren't _really_ 0, you're just reporting them as "negligible" or 0 for convenience.  So I don't think it would make sense to re-fit the model.
A

messages.body_plain:
I think it depends on the application.  For a lot of
large-scale machine learning, like what I used to do in
natural language processing, there are literally billions
of potential predictors.  So in order to get things to fit
into cache (or at least into memory), the number of predictors
is drastically pruned.

It's not like anyone believes the value really is zero in these
cases (just about every aspect of language matters and affects
everything else).

In those cases, for maximum performance, I think it would make sense
to refit.  But maybe there's something else that could be done.

I sent the reference to Aki's paper for some tips on how to do this.

- Bob

messages.subject: prior on gamma model
messages.subject_clean: prior on gamma model
messages.body_plain:
I think this is all fine, except that instead of
shape = mean*rate;
you should have:
rate = shape/mean;
I think this should work.  The idea is that "rate" is just an intermediate quantity; the parameters in the model are "shape", "a", and "b".
A

> On Jul 17, 2016, at 7:50 PM, David J. Harris <harr...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Some collaborators and I are working with a pretty big model, and we're running into some numerical problems with one of the parameters. The model includes a gamma-distributed GLM, which they parameterized in terms of a mean parameter and a rate (inverse scale) parameter:
>
>     mean = exp(a + b * x);
>     shape = mean * rate;
>     y ~ gamma(shape, rate);
>
> This part of the model is giving us some pretty serious numerical problems (e.g. up to 3% of the post-warm-up proposals get rejected because shape is 0, Inf, or NaN, and the remainder of the proposals are very slow when the mean isn't constant).
>
> (I think that these problems are related to the fact that the full model includes a mixture of two very differently-distributed components, and that some of the observations are right-censored. As a result, a lot of observations [especially the imputed observations] fall way out in the right tail where gradients depend on the product of hugely negative conditional likelihoods and very tiny mixture weights.)
>
> I was hoping to keep the shape parameter in a more reasonable range by putting a prior on it:
>
>     shape ~ gamma(4, 1);
>
> When I do this, I get warnings about non-linear transformations. I found the relevant sections of the Stan manual describing "Multivariate Changes of Variables", but I'm not confident enough in multivariate calculus to be sure how to proceed.
>
> In terms of the equations listed in that section, I think my Y is `shape` and my Xs are `a`, `b`, and `rate`.  I know that I can invert the exponent with a logarithm, and I know how to calculate partial derivatives with respect to `a`, `b`, and `rate`, but I'm not totally clear on how to put it all together.  I looked for examples in the manual and in previous stan-users posts, but didn't find anything quite on-point (possibly because my search terms weren't good enough).
>
> Assuming that putting a prior on the shape parameter is a reasonable thing to do, could someone point me toward an example of how I'd go about doing it for parameters of this form?
>
> Thanks so much!
>
> Dave
>

messages.body_plain:
Right, but such dynamic pruning is inherently a greedy
process and it’s really easy to get stuck in local solutions.
Indeed while there are lots of results showing that these
solvers get to the right answer eventually, they sojourn
through all kinds of suboptimal solutions along the way
and there often isn’t a great indication of when you’ve
gone long enough.

Anyways, the point is that these dynamic algorithms
aren’t really Bayesian.  Full Bayes is _not_ a very
sparse approach!

Thanks Andrew!

messages.body_plain:
Well, I would cautiously suggest there is pragmatic value (if not theoretical) even in cases where there are not computational constraints.

A relatively common place example from health psychology (my field) would be examining the effects of stress on health.

Suppose there are:

-         5 continuous stress measures (e.g., domains of family, friends, work, financial, health).

-         10 other sociodemographic factors

Based on previous research it is plausible that:

1)      The effects of stress are non-linear

2)      Stress measures may interact with each other and

3)      Stress measures may interact with the sociodemographic factors

If you only check up to quadratic effects, that still yields: 5 + 10 + 50 = 65 interaction terms.  Each focal stress measure is involved in 15 interactions.  This yields the undesirable result that the threshold for “negligible” must depend on the number of interactions, in way, because even if any one interaction is for all intents and purposes ignorable, the combined set may not be.  Otherwise, even if each individual interaction qualifies as negligible, across the 15 the effects may be large enough that reporting the conditional effect of the stress measure may not be the best estimate of its “overall” effect.  I suppose the correct approach in this case would be to leave all the coefficients as small, non-zero, and marginalize them out to report the overall effect of a stress measure, if they are all sufficiently small (if not the marginal has perhaps little value).  Although conceptually trivial, it is a hassle to actually implement for multiple variables.

Josh

From: Andrew Gelman
Sent: Monday, July 18, 2016 10:58 AM
To: stan-...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: [stan-users] variable selection / spike-and-slab priors forregression coeffs

> On Jul 17, 2016, at 10:05 PM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Well, I would cautiously suggest there is pragmatic value (if not theoretical) even in cases where there are not computational constraints.
>

>
> Suppose there are:
>
> -         5 continuous stress measures (e.g., domains of family, friends, work, financial, health).
>
> -         10 other sociodemographic factors
>
> Based on previous research it is plausible that:
>
> 1)      The effects of stress are non-linear
>
> 2)      Stress measures may interact with each other and
>
> 3)      Stress measures may interact with the sociodemographic factors
>
>
>
> If you only check up to quadratic effects, that still yields: 5 + 10 + 50 = 65 interaction terms.

I don't follow the arithmetic here.

> Each focal stress measure is involved in 15 interactions.  This yields the undesirable result that the threshold for “negligible” must depend on the number of interactions, in way, because even if any one interaction is for all intents and purposes ignorable, the combined set may not be.  Otherwise, even if each individual interaction qualifies as negligible, across the 15 the effects may be large enough that reporting the conditional effect of the stress measure may not be the best estimate of its “overall” effect.  I suppose the correct approach in this case would be to leave all the coefficients as small, non-zero, and marginalize them out to report the overall effect of a stress measure, if they are all sufficiently small (if not the marginal has perhaps little value).

That is the standard Bayesian approach to posterior predictive
inference. The point is that you average predictions over posterior
uncertainty rather than making point estimates of parameters and then
using the point estimates for prediction.  The latter's the norm in most
machine learning applications with which I'm familiar.

It's hard to talk about what is correct without having
an application in mind.  For instance, do you want to make
predictions, estimate "significance", or present as simple
a model as possible?

> Although conceptually trivial, it is a hassle to actually implement for multiple variables.

Why?  I'd think with just 65 it'd be trivial.  Doing anything
other than full Bayes isn't supported by Stan, so doing
some kind of variable selection winds up being more work,
though leads to simpler models in terms of number of parameters.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Jul 17, 2016, at 8:54 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Right, but such dynamic pruning is inherently a greedy
> process and it’s really easy to get stuck in local solutions.
> Indeed while there are lots of results showing that these
> solvers get to the right answer eventually, they sojourn
> through all kinds of suboptimal solutions along the way
> and there often isn’t a great indication of when you’ve
> gone long enough.

I think the usual approach is to just do L1 regularized
regression.  Then there's the problem of setting how much
sparsity you want, leading to those path diagrams favored
by Hastie et al. in their books (and their papers on
elastic net).

> Anyways, the point is that these dynamic algorithms
> aren’t really Bayesian.  Full Bayes is _not_ a very
> sparse approach!

And that's true even with Laplace priors (the distribution
corresponding to L1 regularization).  The posterior isn't
sparse, just the penalized maximum likelihood estimate.

- Bob

> On Jul 17, 2016, at 9:44 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Do you just not understand how to add the Jacobian?
> I would encourage you to consult a probability textbook
> that discusses probability densities and changes of
> variables, but I’ll summarize the basics here.
>
> You want to put a prior on the derived quantity y = f(x).
> Naively you can just substitute f(x) into the density,
>
> p(y) -> p(f(x)),
>
> this this does not define the correct density on x.  Instead
> you need to include the Jacobian,
>
> p(x) = p(f(x)) J(x)
>
> where J(x) =  | dy / dx |.
>
> Or in a Stan program,
>
> parameters {
>   real x;
>   ...
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>   real y;
>   y = f(x);
> }
>
> model {
>   y ~ prior_dist(hyper_parameters);
>   target += log(J(x));
>   ...
> }

messages.body_plain:
On Mon, Jul 18, 2016 at 12:59 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Jul 17, 2016, at 10:05 PM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Well, I would cautiously suggest there is pragmatic value (if not theoretical) even in cases where there are not computational constraints.
> >
> > A relatively common place example from health psychology (my field) would be examining the effects of stress on health.
> >
> > Suppose there are:
> >
> > -         5 continuous stress measures (e.g., domains of family, friends, work, financial, health).
> >
> > -         10 other sociodemographic factors
> >
> > Based on previous research it is plausible that:
> >
> > 1)      The effects of stress are non-linear
> >
> > 2)      Stress measures may interact with each other and
> >
> > 3)      Stress measures may interact with the sociodemographic factors
> >
> >
> >
> > If you only check up to quadratic effects, that still yields: 5 + 10 + 50 = 65 interaction terms.
>
> I don't follow the arithmetic here.

5 squared terms, 10 2-way interactions among the stress measures, and 50 2-way interactions between stress measures and sociodemographic factors, but the number is not important for the example.

>
> > Each focal stress measure is involved in 15 interactions.  This yields the undesirable result that the threshold for “negligible” must depend on the number of interactions, in way, because even if any one interaction is for all intents and purposes ignorable, the combined set may not be.  Otherwise, even if each individual interaction qualifies as negligible, across the 15 the effects may be large enough that reporting the conditional effect of the stress measure may not be the best estimate of its “overall” effect.  I suppose the correct approach in this case would be to leave all the coefficients as small, non-zero, and marginalize them out to report the overall effect of a stress measure, if they are all sufficiently small (if not the marginal has perhaps little value).
>
> That is the standard Bayesian approach to posterior predictive
> inference. The point is that you average predictions over posterior
> uncertainty rather than making point estimates of parameters and then
> using the point estimates for prediction.  The latter's the norm in most
> machine learning applications with which I'm familiar.
>
> It's hard to talk about what is correct without having
> an application in mind.  For instance, do you want to make
> predictions, estimate "significance", or present as simple
> a model as possible?

I had in mind presenting the simplest possible model that captures most of the effects.  Each parameter may inform theory and is conceptually interesting, but to help make sense of data, it is helpful to be parsimonious, when that does not lose much.  I did not have in mind "significance" nor prediction where the interest is in the overall predictive accuracy.

>
> > Although conceptually trivial, it is a hassle to actually implement for multiple variables.
>
> Why?  I'd think with just 65 it'd be trivial.  Doing anything
> other than full Bayes isn't supported by Stan, so doing
> some kind of variable selection winds up being more work,
> though leads to simpler models in terms of number of parameters.

My apologies, I did not explain well.  Here is a simpler and more explicit example:

X is the predictor of interest and is distributed as N(0, 1)
W is a uniformly distributed integer in [0, 10]
f(Y) = 0 + .45*X + 0*W + .01*X*W is equation for the outcome where f() is the link function

The "effect" of X here can be factored as:
(.45 + .01*W)*X

So:
.45 * X | W = 0
.55 * X | W = 10

Since W is uniform, the average marginal effect of X is .50, which is the number I really want to report, not the .45, assuming the interaction terms are sufficiently small.  Unless I am mistaken, for linear outcomes I can get that estimate simply by mean centering all predictors, but I believe it is more complicated for nonlinear outcomes, (e.g., reporting the overall odds ratio or average marginal change in probability from logit link Bernoulli models).
Perhaps this is much simpler than adding a variable selection step, though.  I had in my head, probably erroneously,  that life would be easier if many of the interaction coefficients were true zero instead of just close to zero.

Josh

messages.subject_clean: Multiple datasets with rstan
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to simulate multiple datasets (say 100) and to run stan on each of them (each with 1 chain), to estimate the posterior of a parameter, VE from each of the dataset.

I came across a thread on similar topic and used similar command other users have suggested to do the above.

Here is what it looks like:

fit.est <- stan(file = "2016_07_06_tnd_misclass.stan", data = sdata.list[[1]], init = "random", chains = 1) # compile code

chains <- 100

model.fit <- mclapply(1:chains, FUN = function(chain) {
  stan(fit = fit.est, data = sdata.list[[chain]], chains = 1, verbose = TRUE, warmup = 1000, refresh = -1, iter = 4000, chain_id = chain, seed = 12345, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9, max_treedepth = 15))
}) # update empty object in sim number of way

Can anyone please advise if my command is alright? I have got some results, but quite confident about it.

Also, in my case, as my aim is to estimate posterior from each dataset, do I still need run sflist2stanfit?

Thanks much for advice.

Huiying

On Monday, July 18, 2016 at 1:42:39 AM UTC-4, huiying wrote:
> model.fit <- mclapply(1:chains, FUN = function(chain) {
>   stan(fit = fit.est, data = sdata.list[[chain]], chains = 1, verbose = TRUE, warmup = 1000, refresh = -1, iter = 4000, chain_id = chain, seed = 12345, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9, max_treedepth = 15))
> }) # update empty object in sim number of way
>
>
> Can anyone please advise if my command is alright? I have got some results, but quite confident about it.

You probably want to include mc.cores = parallel::detectCores() and mc.preschedule = FALSE in the call to mclapply(). You will have to see what value of adapt_delta is necessary for these models.

> Also, in my case, as my aim is to estimate posterior from each dataset, do I still need run sflist2stanfit?

No, since sflist2stanfit() is intended for the typical situation where you are conditioning on the same data for all of the chains.

Ben

> Dear Stan Users,
> I am running 4 chains, each with 10,000 steps. When I plot the lp__ of these chains, I found that they are quite flat within the chains, but differ a lot between different chains. I don't quite understand why that happens, and if I want the chains to converge, should I increase the number of chains or the number of steps or anything else?

This is pretty straightforward.  Your model is defining a posterior with multiple modes. The modes are too widely separated (with too deep a valley between them) for the sampler to traverse back and forth so you are not getting convergence (the chains are sampling from different parts of the posterior and you don't get much indication of which part is more important).  This is related to having multiple local optima in optimization but with the added complication that an MCMC sampler can often explore multiple modes so if it is failing to do so the multiple modes are clearly well separated.  Why it's hapenning I can't tell without seeing the model but the typical culprits are mixture models, heavy tailed distributions, particularly for poorly observed parameters, ..., sorry can't come up with the full list but those are the ones I run into most commonly.

Krzysztof

> Thanks,

Do you mean it's more efficient to calculate p separately based on different scenarios? How do I write that?

Let me give you a simple example.

You can write the Bernoulli pmf this way:

  Bernoulli(y | theta) = theta^y * (1 - theta)^(1 - y)

or on the log scale

  log Bernoulli(y | theta) = y * log(theta) + (1 - y) * log(1 - theta)

Either way, it's a lot more work than writing this:

  Bernoulli(y | theta) = y == 0 ? theta : (1 - theta)

or on the log scale

  log Bernoulli(y | theta) = log(y == 0 ? theta : (1 - theta))

or putting it in a conditional.

  real bernoulli(real y, real theta)
  if (y == 0)
    return theta;
  else
    return 1 - theta;

The downside to having four boolean conditions is that you need
sixteen bodies to deal with all the cases if you want to do it within
the Stan program and don't want wasteful multiplications.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I have started looking at your code in a bit more detail. I notice for example that you have

> Overall_Infection_Total[y] <- rep_array(0.001,N_t);

and a comment above

> //Init to non-0, try to banish some nan error messages in lognormal later. (Low count, Ignore it for now.)

You may now have banished the nan error messages :-) You also say you are now using gamma priors and getting convergence. Do you have a git (or other) repo of the latest version of your code? In general, it is quite hard to infer parameters for compartmental models even though one can often get quite good predictions. I'd quite like to investigate this but I'd rather not solve any problems you have already put to bed.

Many thanks, Dominic.

On Thursday, 14 July 2016 04:18:01 UTC+2, David Manheim wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Yes, I was involved in the Dengue modeling project, though good prediction was pretty intractable given the lack of information available; for high fidelity modeling you need lots of location, population, and geography specific data. Some cool ML approaches were tried by various teams with some success, but they require years and years of data to train, and aren't applicable to new locations or changing conditions, so there is limited policy relevance. (And the sponsors basically said they weren't hopeful that Dengue modeling could be advanced all that much.)
>
> I have asked before about time varying inputs, and it's (appropriately) not high on the list of priorities for the core team. I'll be trying gamma priors - my first trial seems to have gotten fairly good convergence, without much fiddling, but that may be luck.
>
> Cheers,
> David
>
> On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 9:57:13 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > Thanks for sharing!  A few comments below. K
> >
> > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 4:28:31 PM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
> > > Hi Krzysztof,
> > >
> > > These are really good points. I do have the model converging, and I'm not finding stability problems anymore - though it took a fair amount of playing with my priors for that to occur consistently across multiple years of data.
> > >
> > > Re: Small numbers and stability, because it is a country level model that represents a single year, with a single implied strain, I am assuming a (low) level of constant baseline infected individuals. This is a kludgy way to account for instability near low numbers, but is effective, and not dissimilar to having an initial infection level. Stochasticity in transmission is a big deal for high fidelity, but for country level models, standard, basic compartmental modeling rarely accounts for it - a known limitation. This is a reason that microsimulation and agent based models are used much more widely now. See my new publication for details! http://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR1576.html (Sorry, I'm really excited about that.)
> >
> > Thanks for mentioning the report, were you involved in the dengue modeling exercise?
> >
> > >
> > > The residuals for the model are comparable to residuals for other ODE models - not great. In this case, the big thing that reduced the systematic discrepancies was accounting for school closures - which I have rarely seen other models do, strangely. (This makes the transmission somewhat time-varying, though in a very specific way.)
> >
> > Thanks for sharing your experience with this.  The systematic patterns in residuals is another feature likely to cause computational problems so it may be a place where introducing time-varying parameters would improve algorithm efficiency enough to offset the extra computational cost.  It would be great to have a plug-in component like the birthday data model for this! Seems like everyone has to re-invent the wheel for dealing with big shocks from holidays.
> >
> > >
> > > Re: lognormal priors, that's a great point. I can change them, and from what I understand, it will probably help. I need a non-negative distribution, so I need to consider which of the several options that Stan now supports I want to use - any suggestions? There are now so many options in the recent versions of Stan!
> >
> > I tend to use gamma priors (and generally spend a lot of time simulating to get the right parameters) or just do more or less standard normal priors and use a scaled logit to get them to cover the right range nicely.  Then you just need to check posterior results to make sure you're not bumping up against the upper end of the range.  There are divergent opinions on this around here so hopefully others will chime in with alternatives but in terms of taking care of computational problems the scaled logit trick works really well as long as you don't have strong background knowledge indicating that values extremely close to zero are likely.
> >
> > Krzysztof
> >
> > >
> > > Thanks for the suggestions,
> > > David
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 2:07:53 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > > > Hi David,
> > > >
> > > > I'm excited to see some of these ODE models for disease in common practice but I've approached it much more
> > > > cautiously.  A colleague at UMass did some basic simulated data for the model Michael (Betancourt) coded up and
> > > > as far as we could tell the numerical performance of that simple model really depends on the parameters used
> > > > to simulate the data.  In general that's sort of a no-brainer but in this case reasonable parameter values seemed
> > > > to make the model hang or fail to converge (this wasn't exhaustive, just trying to get a handle on what needed to
> > > > be done to just be able to throw data sets at these models).  Our other main concern with doing ODE's was that
> > > > in our data sets small counts will sometimes be important and the fact that ODE-based disease models gloss over
> > > > stochasticity in transmission makes me think that there will be serious fit issues (and therefore computational issues)
> > > > unless you introduce time-varying transmission parameters.
> > > >
> > > > So that's a long-winded way of asking whether you got simpler SEIR models working consistently with this type of data (or even simulated data)? Have you looked at residuals for the current fits (even if you don't feel like you have convergence it's useful to see the space the model is exploring and the in-sample predictions it generates).
> > > >
> > > > I'd also be careful about the log-normal priors since they can imply a pretty big upper tail (for example, that lognormal(log(400),5) prior if you simulate a thousand draws will regularly generate values in the 10^8 range which is going to cause computational problems in an ODE model unless there is enough data to make the posterior much tighter.  In a model this complex I have no intuition so I would go with more conservative priors.
> > > >
> > > > I'm sure there are ways to make the computation more efficient too but in my experience issues like lack of fit and priors allowing outlandish parameter values are the first issues to tackle.
> > > >
> > > > Krzysztof
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 11:53:36 AM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
> > > > > Hi all,
> > > > >
> > > > > I have a working model for influenza for my dissertation work, using a SEIR structure based on a model initially provided by Michael Betancourt. My problem is that it's slow / doesn't converge as well as I hoped; this is partially due to complexity, but I think partially due to the structure of the model. I'm hoping people here can help me with a few specific questions, but I'm also open to basically any kind of feedback on the model! I know the model is a bit of a monster, and if anyone has ideas for how to simplify it without removing features of the model, I'd be grateful as well.
> > > > >
> > > > > As a basic intro, I'm fitting 3 different datasets to seasonal flu. The underlying generating mechanism is the differential equation model, and the relationships to the data are a bit complex. I have the 4-compartment, 4-groups SEIR model as an ODE function, and the outputs of the number sick, etc. are used in the model block to be transformed into the actual data, based on some assumptions about the generating mechanism for the data. (Examples: Not all sick people go to the doctor, not all flulike illnesses are actually flue, not all doctors report data, and not all people who visit a doctor have lab tests done - the parameters of each of these are informed by priors.) The model fits the yearly epidemiological flu parameters, the interaction matrix, and the parameterized variables for the relationships between the data and the SEIR model.
> > > > >
> > > > > Specific Questions:
> > > > > 1) Are the transformations to/from matrix form, and to/from array (both in the ODE function, and in the model section) slowing things down significantly? Is there a better way to do this?
> > > > >
> > > > > 2)  Is there a better way to fit the dataset without needing to sample both the transformed parameter vectors, and the actual inputs? (The transformations here are for structural, as opposed to sampling, reasons.)
> > > > >
> > > > > 3) Are there more vectorized ways of doing the looping I have done in the model block? Do they make a big difference?
> > > > >
> > > > > 4) Any suggestions to simplify any other parts of the model structure, without losing the current features?
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks for any potential help / suggestions!
> > > > > David Manheim
> > > > >
> > > > > The model, R Script for running it, and the datasets are attached.

mixture labels aren't identifiable.  So you

If the model's the same, we should get the same MLE.  I'm not
sure what moveHMM does, but I believe they use max marginal
likelihood for some estimates.

That's why I'm worried that either they're fitting a different
model or using a different estimator, or there's something wrong
with the way I coded the HMM.

> Can you confirm the transform you were suggesting is as follows:
>
> parameters {
>     unit_vector[2] xy;  // xy[1]^2 + xy[2]^2 = 1
>
>  transformed parameters {
>     real<lower=-pi(), upper=pi()> theta;
>     theta = atan2(xy[1], xy[2]) - pi();

Yes.   There's an implicit uniform prior on unit vectors,
which means there will be implicitly a uniform prior on theta.

If you want to add a more informative prior, then you'll need
to increment the log density with the log Jacobian determinant
of the transform.

- Bob

messages.subject: Anyone used Stan for implementing a Hierarchical Dirichlet Process mixture model?
messages.subject_clean: Anyone used Stan for implementing a Hierarchical Dirichlet Process mixture model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

We are fairly new to Stan/RStan and would like to implement our Hierarchical Dirichlet Process Mixture model (HDPMM) in Stan.

Our current input data matrix is around 5000 cells (rows) and 1000 genes (columns). Our aim is to cluster these cells based on gene coexpressions (aka gene covariances) but that these covariances are cell-cluster specific. So this is an iterative clustering and normalisation procedure.
The plate model we are referring to is on page 5 (Figure 4) here: http://jmlr.org/proceedings/papers/v48/prabhakaran16.pdf
(Also attached). The model is a HDPMM using Gaussian likelihood. We further scale this Gaussian in both its moments using two scaling parameters: \alpha and \beta.

Questions.
1. Has anyone done DPMM in Stan before? Is it complicated to write down our HDPMM in Stan? I see that the Stan manual (Section 14) discusses regression using Gaussian process.

2. The current input data matrix of 5000 cells and 1000 genes takes around 4-5 hours to converge on naive R (or Matlab).  If we can write our model using Stan, we are hoping to speed this up since Stan uses Hamiltonian MCMC. Is this thought right?

3. If we achieve speed up in Step 2, then we want to scale the model to handle around 100K cells and 20K genes. Would this scale-up be achievable via Stan?

4. We are also considering (Stan's) Variational Bayes.

Our plan is to start writing the HDPMM in Stan as soon as possible and are soliciting any inputs/thoughts into what we need to look or have overlooked. Thank you very much.

Regards,
Sandhya

We can't literally code DPs because Stan uses a fixed

Sorry for the delay.  I'm always hoping other people
will jump in on some of these questions.

You're probably allocating too much memory somewhere.
Stan requires about 24 bytes per function evaluation
plus 8 bytes per argument.  You have at least
D^2 * n^2 loops and some potentially large matrices.

If at all possible, simplifying the matrices to scalar
or smaller matrix operations is much much more efficient.
As is vectorizing wherever possible.

We don't recommend the priors you're using (diffuse inverse
gamma and hard interval constraints [I know Andrew, I owe you
a syntax checker to auto-warn users against these things]) on
statistical (and computational) grounds.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Supervised Classification
messages.body_plain:
Stan will do this all for you pretty much automatically.
The manual has some examples of how to do the predictive
distributions within Stan (that is, you use MCMC for
the integral).

As to the normalized category probabilities, you just
need to normalize:

  vector[K] lp;
  simplex[K] log_theta;

  log_theta = lp - log_sum_exp(lp);

This assumes lp[k] = p(y | k) * p(k),
where p(y|k) is probably of observation given category k
and p(k) is the marginal probability of categories.

Then log_theta[k] is log Pr[C = k | y].

  exp(theta) = exp(lp) / sum(exp(lp))

- Bob

> every class (label) c_i are generated by some normal distribution with unknown \mu_i and \sigma_i specific to class c_i. So for a new text pattern x_new we know that:

>
> P(c_i | x_new, X) = P(x_new | c_i, X) P(c_i) / (\sum_j (P(x_new | c_j, X) P(c_j))
>
> where we can further write P(x_new | c_i, X) = \int d \theta P(x_new | c_i, \theta_i) P(\theta_i | c_i, X) where \theta_i = (\mu_i, \sigma_i)
>
> So to get distribution P(\theta_i|c_i, X) is pretty trivial using the following Stan code:
>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N; // num of training set samples
>     int<lower=1> M; // num of classes
>     real X[N];  //training data

>     int<lower=1, upper=M> C[N]; // class for score n

>    real x_new; //new test pattern to classify
>
> }
> transformed data {}
> parameters {
>     real mu[M];
>     real sigma[M];
>     real x_pred[M];
> }
> transformed parameters {}
> model {
>     //likelihood
>     for (n in 1:N)

>
>     //predictive posterior
>     for (m in 1:M)
>        x_pred[m] ~ normal(mu[m], sigma[m])
>
> }
> generated quantities {
> }

> follows trivially) and then find P(c_i | x_new). What I can do is
>
> generated quantities{
>
>     real x_new_log_likelihood[M];
>     for (m in 1:M)

>         new_score_log_likelihood[m] <- normal_log(x_new)
>
> }
>
> And then in Python calculated the mean of 'new_score_log_likelihood' for every class (actually doing the required transformations because log \sum is not equal to \sum log) and plug in some priors for P(c_i) and just calculate

> P(c_i | x_new) in Python directly. Is there a better way I can do all of this in Stan directly? I hope my explanation is sufficient. I have looked at the
> Naive Bayes example in the manual and I think it should be the same as what I want, but the classification for a new test pattern is not part of the example if I understand
> it correctly.
>
> Regards
> Karl

messages.body_plain:
I’ve seen a few threads recently (one <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/dsHP-BWkjIk/TjZNo0peCAAJ>, two <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/EmkWsppghlg/jl5eii3lBQAJ>, three <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/-OcPLu_kscw/FGKKxwRPBAAJ>, four <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/wf2nQiLG0tQ/NTw1X3dABgAJ>, Github #265 <https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/265>) about inconsistencies in when rstan recompiles a model and when it doesn’t. Most seem to involve reusing a model within the same R session , but I’ve been having trouble even when repeating fully scripted runs in separate sessions.

I think I’ve found a culprit for this, but it’s a weird one. Rstan seems to... always recompile any model that doesn’t end with a newline?

Demo below.

—Chris

-----------

#/!bin/bash

printf '
set.seed(1234)
library(rstan)
rstan_options(auto_write=TRUE)
stanfile = commandArgs(trailingOnly=TRUE)[[1]]
stan(file=stanfile, verbose=TRUE)
# verbose just to make compilation obvious
' > null.R

printf '%b' "data{}parameters{}model{}\n" > null1.stan
printf '%b' "data{}parameters{}model{}" > null2.stan

# First run: both compile as expected
Rscript null.R "null1.stan" > null1.log
Rscript null.R "null2.stan" > null2.log

# Confirm that saved models do exist
ls null*.rda

# Second and subsequent runs:
# null1 run from saved model as expected,
# null2 recompiles every time
# Both models do nothing, as expected.
Rscript null.R "null1.stan" > null1_2.log
Rscript null.R "null2.stan" > null2_2.log
# ...etc...

messages.body_plain:
DP's (and associated mixtures with a DP measure) may be parameterized by unique "locations" and cluster assignments that avoid the multimodality to which you refer and are the bread-and-butter of modern Bayesian estimation (along with other related BNP approaches, such as predictor-indexed DPs and other normalized continuous random measures).    bread. and. butter.  I've successfully implemented a version of a truncated DP mixture in Stan that marginalizes over the mixture indicators as suggested in the stan manual and assigns a Dirichlet(alpha/K,...,alpha/K) prior to the K x 1 vector of mixture probabilities.  This construction contracts on a DP mixture in the limit of K.  I've also constructed an HDP mixture in a similar fashion, but wasn't sure I performed the math correctly.
Anyway, if one's inferential focus is on the parameters on which is imposed a sparsity-induced mixture prior, then the use of this truncated clustering prior approach works well.

terrance.

On Thursday, July 21, 2016 at 7:55:38 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> I was wondering if in the following user-specified function call what the final type of variable c will be:

User-defined functions are templated in the C++ code (except for int) and there is a lot of type promotion. That is the main reason why expose_stan_functions() is so brittle since it has to rewrite everything to only accept doubles from R rather than vars.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
If you're using the function within a Stan program, there is no over-promotion. All the functions are templated on each argument type.

expose_stan_functions() is an rstan function that will bring the Stan program's user-defined functions into the R environment. A call to one of those functions may involve type promotion, if I understand Ben's email, but using user-defined functions within Stan programs do not incur that cost.

Daniel

messages.subject: do the loop portion in translated C++ code in parallel
messages.subject_clean: do the loop portion in translated C++ code in parallel
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have an idea to fast the computing of the stan model. Usually in a complex model with random effect, we need to sample the random effect for each subject, and calculate the likelihood. It would be very time consuming if the data  involves a large number of subjects, but this part can be done independently for each subject. I am thinking doing these parts via GPU parallel computing with thousands of core
thousands of cores
. First, translating the Stan model to C++ code. Then find the loop in the C++ code doing these part of sampling and calculation. Modified that part of code to achieve the same goal in parallel on GPU. Compile the modified code and run the model.
Please let me know whether it is feasible and some guidance to start. I appreciate.

Kan

It would be very time consuming if the data  involves a large number of subjects, but this part can be done independently for each subject. I am thinking doing these parts via GPU parallel computing with thousands of core
> thousands of cores

That is currently only realistic in specific cases. If the likelihood does not utilize autodiff (i.e. all the var inputs are stripped down to doubles, the score is calculated analytically, and the derivative information is reattached to the output), it could be done but the likelihood evaluation for each observation would need to take a long time to overcome the repeated offloading to the GPU and the summation on the CPU of all the pieces returned by the GPU. We don't have any way to determine that automatically, so it would have to be something done by a human.  Also, GPU operations are more advanced for floats than doubles, but Stan does not do floats.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi, just to be clear:  if you write the model in Stan you can fit it right away using NUTS (i.e., full Bayes), and I recommend you start with that, i.e. start with a model that is not too large and fit full Bayes.  This should be faster and more scalable than any Gibbs sampler implementation you might have.  At that point you can run Stan using ADVI (that is, variational Bayes); no additional programming is required.  But I recommend you first do the full Bayes on a reasonable-sized problem, then do ADVI and compare.  You can do it all within Stan.
A

>
> For locking in particular observations in an HMM, do you mean

>

>
>> On Jul 20, 2016, at 8:04 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

>> Never "just use a single chain."  If you can't identify the mixture components by ordering their means, you can identify them by locking in particular observations to particular components.  Or there are other ways of doing it.

>>>

>>>
>>> Depends what you're doing.  The problem is that the
>>> mixture labels aren't identifiable.  So you
>>> either need to insure the model's identifiable (say by
>>> ordering means of components or something) or just use
>>> a single chain or just do inference that doesn't depend on
>>> the identity of mixture components.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>>
>>>> For completeness, the code below is what I've been using to generate the fake data:
>>>>
>>>> ## Generate a continuous latent variable that we then use to make a discrete state vector
>>>> fARProcess <- function(rho,X0,sigma,aT){
>>>> X <- vector(length=aT)
>>>> X[1] <- X0
>>>> for(t in 2:aT){
>>>>  X[t] = rho * X[t-1] + rnorm(1,0,sigma)
>>>> }
>>>> return(X)
>>>> }
>>>>
>>>> fState <- function(rho,X0,sigma,aT){
>>>> X <- fARProcess(rho,X0,sigma,aT)
>>>> Z <- ifelse(X<0,0,1)
>>>> return(Z)
>>>> }

>>>>    l[t] <- rweibull(1,aAlpha,aBeta1)

>>>> }

>>>> return(lAngle)

No. But you would be comparing it to an overly slow version anyway. This line

for ( j in 1:N_herd_index ) vary_herd_index[j] ~ normal( 0 , sigma_herd_index );

should just be

vary_herd_index ~ normal( 0 , sigma_herd_index );

which evaluates very quickly on a CPU. None of the basic univariate density functions with accumulating analytical derivatives are going to evaluate slowly enough to justify the trip to a GPU and then summing the results on a GPU. It might be worthwhile if you are doing a multivariate normal density with 10000 dimensions or integrating an ODE for each person or something.

Ben

Pr[C = k | x_new, x, y] is a single value, but then it's a vector
when you consider all k values.

The final output is a sample from the posterior consisting of
a sequence of draws.  You can get a single expectation by
averaging, and you can also get uncertainty in that estimate by
looking at quantiles.  It's standard posterior predictive inference,
which averages over the posterior.

  Pr[C = k | x_new, x, y]

  = INTEGRAL_theta Pr[C = k | x_new, theta] p(theta | x, y) d.theta

where theta are your parameters.

- Bob
