> On Jul 17, 2016, at 7:50 PM, David J. Harris <harr...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Some collaborators and I are working with a pretty big model, and we're running into some numerical problems with one of the parameters. The model includes a gamma-distributed GLM, which they parameterized in terms of a mean parameter and a rate (inverse scale) parameter:
>
>     mean = exp(a + b * x);
>     shape = mean * rate;
>     y ~ gamma(shape, rate);

I'm guessing you want to declare Stan parameters (a, b, mean, rate)
and thus the program will define a density p(a, b, mean, rate).
Then you define shape as a transformed parameter as above.

  shape = mean * rate;

That means your transform is

  (a, b, mean, rate) |--> (a, b, mean, shape)

Then you want to define the model in terms of a density on
p(a, b, mean, shape).

   a ~ ...;
   b ~ ...;
   mean ~ ...;
   shape ~ ...;

Because the mapping from (a, b, mean) to (a, b, mean) is the identity,
the Jacobian's automaticaly lower triangular, so the Jacobian is
the product of the diagonal entries.  The diagonal entries in the
Jacobian matrix are just

  d.a / d.a = 1
  d.b / d.b = 1
  d.mean / d.mean = 1
  d.shape / d.rate = mean

and the Jacobian determinant the product of the diagonal

  |J| = abs(1 * 1 * 1 * mean)

with absolute value

  |J| = abs(mean)

and the adjustment is then

  log |J| = log(mean)

and the Jacobian can be expressed in Stan on the log scale is just

  target += log(fabs(mean));

I think mean > 0 here, right, so you can drop the fabs function.

You'll want to double-check my work here.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Avoid data discretization - for prior dependent on x
messages.subject_clean: Avoid data discretization - for prior dependent on x
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, July 23, 2016 at 3:53:51 AM UTC-4, Jan wrote:
> Seems interesting! So it's kernel statistics and/or qr decomposition. It something that I'm not familiar with so so far i cannot translate such info into my model. I'm reading about it, but if you have some code for doing it would be great.

If you use R, then you can just do

X <- poly(predictor, degree = 2, raw = TRUE)
xbar <- colMeans(X)
X <- sweep(X, 2, xbar)
QR <- qr(X)
Q <- qr.Q(QR)
R <- qr.R(QR)

then pass the two columns of Q to Stan and modify your Stan code to be

y ~ gamma(q1 * alpha_1 + q2 * alpha_2 + alpha_3, q1 * beta_1 + q2 * beta_2 + beta_3);

To interpret the coefficients in terms of X, you have to pre-multiply them by the inverse of R.

Ben

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Truncated normal distribution problem
messages.body_plain:
On another note, you can avoid declaring the variance as a transformed parameter and directly put a prior on sigma. That's usually advisable for several reasons. It avoids unnecessary computation (that's just a tiny benefit here) but more importantly sd is in the same units as y and so it's often easier to conceptualize what the prior on sigma implies. We also don't recommend those inverse-gamma priors as they are advertised as non-informative but really aren't. There's more on that topic in the manual and in Andrew's 2006 paper (cited in the manual).

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
You can think of setting them to single values as being
an approximate Bayesian technique.  Fixing hyperparameters
tends to underestimate posterior uncertainty compared to
estimating them along with other parameters.  In estimating
then fixing the hyperparameters, this is related to empirical
Bayes (another approximate Bayesian inference technique, often
carried out with max marginal likelihood).

- Bob

> On Jul 21, 2016, at 2:44 PM, Charles Driver <cdriv...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Well, instead of sampling the hyper correlations I am now setting them deterministically based on the correlation of the sampled lower level parameters...  this is working great from a computational / empirical perspective, have you seen such an approach or have any thoughts on how one might justify it? I would be unsure about the relation between the posterior of the determined correlations and the 'true / sampled correlation' posterior, so wouldn't lean on the correlations for inferential purposes, but other than that I would expect things to be 'fine'...
>
> On Monday, July 18, 2016 at 11:07:59 PM UTC+2, Charles Driver wrote:
> I guess that would be one way out, seems a little ugly but maybe not more so in reality than the other model decisions...

>>

Hi Yang,

Glad that's working for you now.

I don't know the hBayesDM package, but we definitely recommend running more than three chains. I see you have chains=3 but 5000 iterations per chain. Typically you'll want at least 4 chains but need fewer iterations (our somewhat conservative default -- for NUTS sampler only -- is 1000 warmup + 1000 sampling per chain). For some models you'll need to increase the number of iterations, but rarely if ever do you want to be decreasing the number of chains. The more chains you run the better chance you have of discovering pathological regions of the posterior that shouldn't be ignored.

Jonah

> On Jul 17, 2016, at 10:05 PM, Joshua Wiley <jwiley...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Well, I would cautiously suggest there is pragmatic value (if not theoretical) even in cases where there are not computational constraints.
> A relatively common place example from health psychology (my field) would be examining the effects of stress on health.
> Suppose there are:
> -         5 continuous stress measures (e.g., domains of family, friends, work, financial, health).
> -         10 other sociodemographic factors
> Based on previous research it is plausible that:
> 1)      The effects of stress are non-linear
> 2)      Stress measures may interact with each other and
> 3)      Stress measures may interact with the sociodemographic factors
>
> If you only check up to quadratic effects, that still yields: 5 + 10 + 50 = 65 interaction terms.  Each focal stress measure is involved in 15 interactions.  This yields the undesirable result that the threshold for “negligible” must depend on the number of interactions, in way, because even if any one interaction is for all intents and purposes ignorable, the combined set may not be.  Otherwise, even if each individual interaction qualifies as negligible, across the 15 the effects may be large enough that reporting the conditional effect of the stress measure may not be the best estimate of its “overall” effect.  I suppose the correct approach in this case would be to leave all the coefficients as small, non-zero, and marginalize them out to report the overall effect of a stress measure, if they are all sufficiently small (if not the marginal has perhaps little value).  Although conceptually trivial, it is a hassle to actually implement for multiple variables.

messages.subject_clean: constrain array of vectors in [0,x], x <= 1
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

since in STAN we cannot put constrains on each element of a vector,
in sense of limit each vector in [0,x], x <= 1. Suppose we have
V vectors with D-1 dimensions, then I come up with following
solution. I defined:

simplex[D] alpha[V];

I consider alpha[i,D] as the interval [x,1] which we don't use.
We could additionally put a dirchlet-prior onto alpha[i]. I do it's
estimate with:

library(VGAM)
ddata=data.frame(alpha)
fit <- vglm(cbind(alpha0, alpha1, alpha2) ~ 1, dirichlet,
data = ddata, trace = TRUE, crit = "coef")
Coef(fit)

Alternative
I know we could also define the vector by D-1 and then scale
it.

Any hints, advises are most welcome,
Andre

> Hi,
>
> since in STAN we cannot put constrains on each element of a vector,
> in sense of limit each vector in [0,x], x <= 1. Suppose we have
> V vectors with D-1 dimensions, then I come up with following
> solution. I defined:
>
> simplex[D] alpha[V];
>
> I consider alpha[i,D] as the interval [x,1] which we don't use.
> We could additionally put a dirchlet-prior onto alpha[i]. I do it's
> estimate with:
>
> library(VGAM)
> ddata=data.frame(alpha)
> fit <- vglm(cbind(alpha0, alpha1, alpha2) ~ 1, dirichlet,
> data = ddata, trace = TRUE, crit = "coef")
> Coef(fit)
>
> Alternative
> I know we could also define the vector by D-1 and then scale
> it.
>
> Any hints, advises are most welcome,
> Andre

Hi,

What do you mean when you say that sigma_theta never converges? Mind describing what diagnostics you're looking at to say that?

Daniel

On Mon, Jul 25, 2016 at 6:03 AM, Christopher Claassen <chris.c...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> I am working on estimating latent national public opinion ("theta") for 126 countries over 25 years using around 3000 observed nationally-aggregated responses to 33 survey questions drawn from across these countries and years.
>
> The model, below, is mostly working fine, except for the autoregressive / dynamic component. I treat this as a random walk, so theta[t,j] ~ normal(theta[t-1,j], sigma_theta), for t time periods and j countries.
>
> The trouble is with sigma_theta, the evolution parameter. The sampled values hover around a reasonable value (0.03) with Rhats in the 1.3-1.4 range. But it
> never converges even as the rest of the model settles down pretty quickly (within say 1000 iterations and 4 chains).
>
> I suppose I could just throw 5000 iterations at the problem, but I suspect there is some issue with identification.
>
> I began with a half-cauchy(0, 2) prior but am now using a half-normal(0, 0.5), which appears marginally better.
>
> Thanks in advance for any comments or suggestions
>
>
> data{
>   int<lower=1> N;               // number of national survey opinions
>   int<lower=1> J;               // number of countries
>   int<lower=1> K;            // number of items by project
>   int<lower=1> T;            // number of years
>   int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N];   // country j for opinion n
>   int<lower=1,upper=K> kk[N];   // item-project k for opinion n
>   int<lower=1,upper=T> tt[N];   // year t for opinion n
>   real xsq[N];    // vector of survey opinions, 0-1, squared
> }
>
> parameters{
>   matrix[T,J] theta;                  // matrix of T by J latent traits
>   vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_eps;  // K item-project-specific residual error variances
>   real<lower=0> sigma_theta;         // opinion evolution error variance
>   vector[K-1] alpha_est;                // estimated item-project location parameters
>   real<lower=0> sigma_alpha;     // item-project-level error variance
>   real mu_alpha;             // expectation of item-project location pars
> }
>
> transformed parameters{
>   real x_hat[N];                 // fitted values
>   vector<lower=0>[N] sigma_eps_kk; // N-expanded residual error variances
>   vector[K] alpha;                      // item-project location parameters
>   alpha[1] <- .575; // constrain 1st loc. par. to observed mean
>   alpha[2:K] <- alpha_est[1:(K-1)];     // map item location params to alpha vector
>   sigma_eps_kk <- sigma_eps[kk];
>   for (i in 1:N)  // fitted values model
>     x_hat[i] <- alpha[kk[i]] + theta[tt[i],jj[i]];
> }
>
> model{
>   theta[1] ~ normal(0, 0.5); // latent trait evolution model
>   to_vector(theta[2:T]) ~ normal(to_vector(theta[1:(T-1)]), sigma_theta);
>   xsq ~ normal(x_hat, sigma_eps_kk);  // response model
>   alpha_est ~ normal(mu_alpha, sigma_alpha);
>   sigma_theta ~ normal(0, 0.5);
>   sigma_alpha ~ cauchy(0, 2);
>   sigma_eps ~ cauchy(0, 2);
>   mu_alpha ~ normal(0, 2);
> }
>
> generated quantities {
>   vector[N] x_pred;
>   for (i in 1:N)         // simulate fitted data to check model
>     x_pred[i] <- normal_rng(x_hat[i], sigma_eps_kk[i]);

messages.body_plain:
I just wrote a response on how to do this, and am working on
adding general upper and lower bound constraints, which I'll cut
and paste here:

So you can declare

parameters {
 vector[N] l_p_raw;

and then have transformed parameters (assuming U[i] is
upper bound and L[i] lower bound:

transformed parameters {
 vector[N] l_p;
 for (n in 1:N)
   l_p[n] = (U[n] - L[n]) * inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) + U[n];

model {
 target += log((U[n] - L[n]) * inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) * (1 - inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]));

That's not the most efficient way to implement things, but it should
work if values aren't too extreme.  Otherwise you want
to use

 target+= log(U[n] - L[n]) + log_inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]) + log1m_inv_logit(l_p_raw[n]);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Lily,

it seems like sometimes, the 'u' value is too large or too small. You can try to print the variable by using the print() function.

Anyways, there are several places you could modify/improve.

(1)
instead of using:
          pchoice <- inv_logit(mu[ID]*u);
          choice[ID, t] ~ bernoulli(pchoice);
try:
          choice[ID, t] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu[ID]*u);

(2)
instead of declaring:
          for (i in 1:N) {
              alpha[i]     <- 2 * alpha_p[i];
try vectorizing it:
          alpha     <- 2 * alpha_p;

(3)
when assigning a negative value, please leave a space.
Do:
          us[j] <-  (-lambda[ID]) * pow((-vs[j]), beta[ID]);
instead of :
          us[j] <-(-lambda[ID]) * pow((-vs[j]), beta[ID]);

(4)
you could follow Stan Reference (2.9, P174) to reparameterize the prior of your beta distribution.

Hope this helps.

L.

messages.body_plain:
Hey all:

New group member and relatively new Stan user here.  I apologize if this has been asked before or if I am asking something obvious.

I have a modeling situation where I want to define several simplex parameter vectors.  They could potentially be of different dimensions, and the dimensions (or, in fact, how many there will be) will not be known until the data are read in.  So I have been trying to think of a way defining them generally, calling each one something like lambda[i], i=1, ..., n for the n simplexes I need.

I was thinking that an array specification might work as in

simplex[J] lambda[n];

except for the fact that J would not be the same for each i = 1, ..., n.

Is there some work-around that you can suggest?  Indeed would this work:

simplex[m[i]] lambda[n];

where m[i] specifies the dimension of the ith simplex?  I did not think so, since all the examples suggest that the array would need a constant "number of columns."  I was thinking that the list type in R would handle this well, but I do not see how I can get an equivalent in Stan.

Thanks in advance,
Bruce Allen

See inline comments below.

> On Jul 25, 2016, at 10:38 AM, Lei Zhang <bnuzhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Lily,
>
> it seems like sometimes, the 'u' value is too large or too small. You can try to print the variable by using the print() function.
>
> Anyways, there are several places you could modify/improve.
>
> (1)
> instead of using:
>           pchoice <- inv_logit(mu[ID]*u);
>           choice[ID, t] ~ bernoulli(pchoice);
> try:
>           choice[ID, t] ~ bernoulli_logit(mu[ID]*u);

This won't affect efficiency, so it's more a matter of style.

>
> (2)
> instead of declaring:
>           for (i in 1:N) {
>               alpha[i]     <- 2 * alpha_p[i];
> try vectorizing it:
>           alpha     <- 2 * alpha_p;

This one's all good.  Vectorizing is more efficient and I think
the code's clearer.

>
> (3)
> when assigning a negative value, please leave a space.
> Do:
>           us[j] <-  (-lambda[ID]) * pow((-vs[j]), beta[ID]);
> instead of :
>           us[j] <-(-lambda[ID]) * pow((-vs[j]), beta[ID]);

You don't need the first set of parens, so I'd just use this:

  us[j] = -lambda[ID] * (-vs[j])^beta[ID];

vs[j] will have to be negative here or the answers aren't going
to make sense.

But I'm worried that you're using an index ID that's not
part of the left-hand side.

- Bob

On Tuesday, July 19, 2016 at 7:20:29 AM UTC-4, idontgetoutmuch wrote:
> Hi David,
>
> I have started looking at your code in a bit more detail. I notice for example that you have
>
> > Overall_Infection_Total[y] <- rep_array(0.001,N_t);
>
> and a comment above
>
> > //Init to non-0, try to banish some nan error messages in lognormal later. (Low count, Ignore it for now.)
>
> You may now have banished the nan error messages :-) You also say you are now using gamma priors and getting convergence. Do you have a git (or other) repo of the latest version of your code? In general, it is quite hard to infer parameters for compartmental models even though one can often get quite good predictions. I'd quite like to investigate this but I'd rather not solve any problems you have already put to bed.
>
> Many thanks, Dominic.
>
> On Thursday, 14 July 2016 04:18:01 UTC+2, David Manheim wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > Yes, I was involved in the Dengue modeling project, though good prediction was pretty intractable given the lack of information available; for high fidelity modeling you need lots of location, population, and geography specific data. Some cool ML approaches were tried by various teams with some success, but they require years and years of data to train, and aren't applicable to new locations or changing conditions, so there is limited policy relevance. (And the sponsors basically said they weren't hopeful that Dengue modeling could be advanced all that much.)
> >
> > I have asked before about time varying inputs, and it's (appropriately) not high on the list of priorities for the core team. I'll be trying gamma priors - my first trial seems to have gotten fairly good convergence, without much fiddling, but that may be luck.
> >
> > Cheers,
> > David
> >
> > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 9:57:13 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > > Thanks for sharing!  A few comments below. K
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 4:28:31 PM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
> > > > Hi Krzysztof,
> > > >
> > > > These are really good points. I do have the model converging, and I'm not finding stability problems anymore - though it took a fair amount of playing with my priors for that to occur consistently across multiple years of data.
> > > >
> > > > Re: Small numbers and stability, because it is a country level model that represents a single year, with a single implied strain, I am assuming a (low) level of constant baseline infected individuals. This is a kludgy way to account for instability near low numbers, but is effective, and not dissimilar to having an initial infection level. Stochasticity in transmission is a big deal for high fidelity, but for country level models, standard, basic compartmental modeling rarely accounts for it - a known limitation. This is a reason that microsimulation and agent based models are used much more widely now. See my new publication for details! http://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RR1576.html (Sorry, I'm really excited about that.)
> > >
> > > Thanks for mentioning the report, were you involved in the dengue modeling exercise?
> > >
> > > >
> > > > The residuals for the model are comparable to residuals for other ODE models - not great. In this case, the big thing that reduced the systematic discrepancies was accounting for school closures - which I have rarely seen other models do, strangely. (This makes the transmission somewhat time-varying, though in a very specific way.)
> > >
> > > Thanks for sharing your experience with this.  The systematic patterns in residuals is another feature likely to cause computational problems so it may be a place where introducing time-varying parameters would improve algorithm efficiency enough to offset the extra computational cost.  It would be great to have a plug-in component like the birthday data model for this! Seems like everyone has to re-invent the wheel for dealing with big shocks from holidays.
> > >
> > > >
> > > > Re: lognormal priors, that's a great point. I can change them, and from what I understand, it will probably help. I need a non-negative distribution, so I need to consider which of the several options that Stan now supports I want to use - any suggestions? There are now so many options in the recent versions of Stan!
> > >
> > > I tend to use gamma priors (and generally spend a lot of time simulating to get the right parameters) or just do more or less standard normal priors and use a scaled logit to get them to cover the right range nicely.  Then you just need to check posterior results to make sure you're not bumping up against the upper end of the range.  There are divergent opinions on this around here so hopefully others will chime in with alternatives but in terms of taking care of computational problems the scaled logit trick works really well as long as you don't have strong background knowledge indicating that values extremely close to zero are likely.
> > >
> > > Krzysztof
> > >
> > > >
> > > > Thanks for the suggestions,
> > > > David
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 2:07:53 PM UTC-4, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> > > > > Hi David,
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm excited to see some of these ODE models for disease in common practice but I've approached it much more
> > > > > cautiously.  A colleague at UMass did some basic simulated data for the model Michael (Betancourt) coded up and
> > > > > as far as we could tell the numerical performance of that simple model really depends on the parameters used
> > > > > to simulate the data.  In general that's sort of a no-brainer but in this case reasonable parameter values seemed
> > > > > to make the model hang or fail to converge (this wasn't exhaustive, just trying to get a handle on what needed to
> > > > > be done to just be able to throw data sets at these models).  Our other main concern with doing ODE's was that
> > > > > in our data sets small counts will sometimes be important and the fact that ODE-based disease models gloss over
> > > > > stochasticity in transmission makes me think that there will be serious fit issues (and therefore computational issues)
> > > > > unless you introduce time-varying transmission parameters.
> > > > >
> > > > > So that's a long-winded way of asking whether you got simpler SEIR models working consistently with this type of data (or even simulated data)? Have you looked at residuals for the current fits (even if you don't feel like you have convergence it's useful to see the space the model is exploring and the in-sample predictions it generates).
> > > > >
> > > > > I'd also be careful about the log-normal priors since they can imply a pretty big upper tail (for example, that lognormal(log(400),5) prior if you simulate a thousand draws will regularly generate values in the 10^8 range which is going to cause computational problems in an ODE model unless there is enough data to make the posterior much tighter.  In a model this complex I have no intuition so I would go with more conservative priors.
> > > > >
> > > > > I'm sure there are ways to make the computation more efficient too but in my experience issues like lack of fit and priors allowing outlandish parameter values are the first issues to tackle.
> > > > >
> > > > > Krzysztof
> > > > >
> > > > > On Tuesday, July 12, 2016 at 11:53:36 AM UTC-4, David Manheim wrote:
> > > > > > Hi all,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I have a working model for influenza for my dissertation work, using a SEIR structure based on a model initially provided by Michael Betancourt. My problem is that it's slow / doesn't converge as well as I hoped; this is partially due to complexity, but I think partially due to the structure of the model. I'm hoping people here can help me with a few specific questions, but I'm also open to basically any kind of feedback on the model! I know the model is a bit of a monster, and if anyone has ideas for how to simplify it without removing features of the model, I'd be grateful as well.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > As a basic intro, I'm fitting 3 different datasets to seasonal flu. The underlying generating mechanism is the differential equation model, and the relationships to the data are a bit complex. I have the 4-compartment, 4-groups SEIR model as an ODE function, and the outputs of the number sick, etc. are used in the model block to be transformed into the actual data, based on some assumptions about the generating mechanism for the data. (Examples: Not all sick people go to the doctor, not all flulike illnesses are actually flue, not all doctors report data, and not all people who visit a doctor have lab tests done - the parameters of each of these are informed by priors.) The model fits the yearly epidemiological flu parameters, the interaction matrix, and the parameterized variables for the relationships between the data and the SEIR model.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Specific Questions:
> > > > > > 1) Are the transformations to/from matrix form, and to/from array (both in the ODE function, and in the model section) slowing things down significantly? Is there a better way to do this?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 2)  Is there a better way to fit the dataset without needing to sample both the transformed parameter vectors, and the actual inputs? (The transformations here are for structural, as opposed to sampling, reasons.)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 3) Are there more vectorized ways of doing the looping I have done in the model block? Do they make a big difference?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > 4) Any suggestions to simplify any other parts of the model structure, without losing the current features?
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks for any potential help / suggestions!
> > > > > > David Manheim
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The model, R Script for running it, and the datasets are attached.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How can I avoid exponentiating a vector by a vector?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How can I avoid exponentiating a vector by a vector?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks a lot for getting back to me. I'll try and elaborate efficiently.

I'm trying to fit an overdispersed Poisson loglinear regression to some counts of duck abundance. I want to partition error inherent in the counts into relevant components: region effects (parameterized with a subset of USFWS Regions), random year effects, observer effects, sampling unit effects, and a noise term that accounts for variable effort in surveys (parameterized with the length of the survey in hours). So, every count 'i' is modeled as,

count[i] = region[R[i]] + year[Y[i]] + observer[O[i]] + unit[U[i]] + effort[i],

and the data used to inform the model look like the example data attached ('stan_help_example_data.txt').

Region, Year, Observer, and Unit are all treated as normally distributed parameters with mean = 0 and variance ~ gamma(0.001,0.001).

Effort is a transformed parameter calculated using survey length and two additional region-specific parameters, B and p (following the convention of a model built by Bill Link, John Sauer, and Dan Niven):

effort[i] = B[R[i]] * { [ ( survey_length[i] / mean(survey_length[]) ) ^ p[R[i]] ] - 1 } / p[R[i]].

I've coded all of this in BUGS, and the model technically runs, but it takes 3 days when it does run, and it's very tricky to choose appropriate initial values and get the model to converge. So I'm switching to Stan to see if it can offer any improvement. The main problem I'm having with the transition is keeping track of indexing. Since every count is associated with a particular region, year, observer, and unit, in BUGS I can use 'for' loops to identify each of these by count. As in:

for( i in 1:ncounts) {
     mu[i] <- region[R[i]] + year[Y[i]] + observer[O[i]] + unit[U[i]] + effort[i]
     lambda[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau)
     count[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
     tau ~ dgamma(0.001,0.001)
}

 Since region, year, observer, and unit all have relatively straightforward priors, coding those in Stan is equivalently straightforward. Coding effort is where my hang up is. In BUGS, I write:

for( i in 1:ncounts) {
     effort[i] <- B[R[i]] * ( ( ( ( survey_length[i] / mean(survey_length[]) ) ^ p[R[i]] ) - 1 ) / p[R[i]] )
},

as above. Since the dataset has number of rows = 'ncounts', it simply iterates through the dataset by 'i', and informs 'R' with the associated region. So, using the example data, when 'i' = 86, 'R' = 1, and BUGS relays this to 'B' as B[R[86]] = B[1] (similarly for p[R[86]] = p[1]).

In trying to convert this to Stan, I've tried leveraging the native vector capabilities within Stan, and I've tried explicitly indexing by 'R' and 'i'. The former approach (see attached file, 'iwmm_effort_model_vectorized.stan') has resulted in fatal errors, and the latter (see attached file 'iwmm_effort_model.stan') has allowed the model to "run", but it still takes a comparable amount of time to running it in BUGS, and to run a sufficient number of iterations to achieve convergence (~1000, I'm guessing), I end up running out of RAM (after 500 iterations over 3 chains). I'm trying to run it now with just 2 chains and 200 iterations, but R is hanging without even showing evidence of having parsed the model.

My basic problem (I think), is that I don't know how to perform the similar translation in Stan that I did in BUGS with B[R[i]] (and p[R[i]]). I'm assuming that, since this is my first Stan model, I'm thinking about the indexing wrong, and there may be a simpler (and better) way to think about this, and even a simpler/better way to format the data. I'd really like to optimize the code and take advantage of Stan's vectorization utilities, but perhaps I'm constrained in that approach.

Kevin

On Monday, July 25, 2016 at 2:43:22 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Jul 25, 2016, at 2:05 PM, Kevin Aagaard <kevin.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >
> > Hello,
> >
> > As a disclaimer, this is the first model I've written with Stan.
> >
> > I'm having difficulty overcoming the exponentiation of a vector by a vector, as seen in line 64 of the attached script:
> >
> > effort = B * ((ScaledEffort ^ p) - 1) / p;
> >
> > which yields the following error: "arguments to ^ must be primitive (real or int); cannot exponentiate vector by vector".
> >
> > I've tried converting this to:
> >
> > for(i in 1:ncounts) {
> >  effort[i] =
> >    B[regions[i]] * ((ScaledEffort[i] ^ p[regions[i]]) - 1) / p[regions[i]];
> > }
> >
>
> That's not the same as the above, because of the regions inside of B.
> So I'm not sure what your intent is here.
>
> >
> > to force element-wise exponentiation (as suggested in this discussion), but that yielded this error: "Exception thrown at line 92: stan::math::normal_log: Location parameter has dimension = 1, expecting dimension = 3; a function was called with arguments of different scalar, array, vector, or matrix types, and they were not consistently sized;  all arguments must be scalars or multidimensional values of the same shape."
> >
> > This new error refers to this line:
> >
> > B ~ normal(B_mu, B_sigma);
> >
> > which apparently now has only dimension=1 instead of dimension=3 (corresponding to the number of regions across which the data are spread).
>
> All of the arguments to a sampling statement must have
> the same size, or must be scalars.  So figure out which
> two of these have different errors.  It helps in general
> if you can report the exact error message, because without
> it, we're guessing.
>
> - Bob
>

> On Jul 26, 2016, at 10:46 AM, Kevin Aagaard <kevin.j...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks a lot for getting back to me. I'll try and elaborate efficiently.
>
> I'm trying to fit an overdispersed Poisson loglinear regression to some counts of duck abundance. I want to partition error inherent in the counts into relevant components: region effects (parameterized with a subset of USFWS Regions), random year effects, observer effects, sampling unit effects, and a noise term that accounts for variable effort in surveys (parameterized with the length of the survey in hours). So, every count 'i' is modeled as,
>
> count[i] = region[R[i]] + year[Y[i]] + observer[O[i]] + unit[U[i]] + effort[i],
>
> and the data used to inform the model look like the example data attached ('stan_help_example_data.txt').
>
> Region, Year, Observer, and Unit are all treated as normally distributed parameters with mean = 0 and variance ~ gamma(0.001,0.001).
>
> Effort is a transformed parameter calculated using survey length and two additional region-specific parameters, B and p (following the convention of a model built by Bill Link, John Sauer, and Dan Niven):
>
> effort[i] = B[R[i]] * { [ ( survey_length[i] / mean(survey_length[]) ) ^ p[R[i]] ] - 1 } / p[R[i]].
>
> I've coded all of this in BUGS, and the model technically runs, but it takes 3 days when it does run, and it's very tricky to choose appropriate initial values and get the model to converge. So I'm switching to Stan to see if it can offer any improvement. The main problem I'm having with the transition is keeping track of indexing. Since every count is associated with a particular region, year, observer, and unit, in BUGS I can use 'for' loops to identify each of these by count. As in:
>
> for( i in 1:ncounts) {
>      mu[i] <- region[R[i]] + year[Y[i]] + observer[O[i]] + unit[U[i]] + effort[i]
>      lambda[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau)
>      count[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])
>      tau ~ dgamma(0.001,0.001)
> }

You can code this exactly the same way in Stan.  The above
won't work in BUGS because you have tau defined multiple times
as a stochastic node.  Also, those gamma(0.001, 0.001) priors
are bad news.  You can code priors directly on scale in Stan (or
in BUGS).

>
>  Since region, year, observer, and unit all have relatively straightforward priors, coding those in Stan is equivalently straightforward. Coding effort is where my hang up is. In BUGS, I write:
>
> for( i in 1:ncounts) {
>      effort[i] <- B[R[i]] * ( ( ( ( survey_length[i] / mean(survey_length[]) ) ^ p[R[i]] ) - 1 ) / p[R[i]] )
> },
>
> as above. Since the dataset has number of rows = 'ncounts', it simply iterates through the dataset by 'i', and informs 'R' with the associated region. So, using the example data, when 'i' = 86, 'R' = 1, and BUGS relays this to 'B' as B[R[86]] = B[1] (similarly for p[R[86]] = p[1]).
>
> In trying to convert this to Stan, I've tried leveraging the native vector capabilities within Stan, and I've tried explicitly indexing by 'R' and 'i'. The former approach (see attached file, 'iwmm_effort_model_vectorized.stan') has resulted in fatal errors, and the latter (see attached file 'iwmm_effort_model.stan') has allowed the model to "run", but it still takes a comparable amount of time to running it in BUGS,

As measured by n_eff per unit of time or in terms of iterations?

> and to run a sufficient number of iterations to achieve convergence (~1000, I'm guessing), I end up running out of RAM (after 500 iterations over 3 chains). I'm trying to run it now with just 2 chains and 200 iterations, but R is hanging without even showing evidence of having parsed the model.
>
> My basic problem (I think), is that I don't know how to perform the similar translation in Stan that I did in BUGS with B[R[i]] (and p[R[i]]).

I'd suggest starting by translating the BUGS model line for line.

> I'm assuming that, since this is my first Stan model, I'm thinking about the indexing wrong, and there may be a simpler (and better) way to think about this, and even a simpler/better way to format the data. I'd really like to optimize the code and take advantage of Stan's vectorization utilities, but perhaps I'm constrained in that approach.

There may be, but I still don't understand where your problem
is.  If you have a working Stan program, it's much easier to
help you improve it than it is to try to debug it without
really understanding what the goal is.

- Bob

messages.subject: can I make posterior predictions in rstanarm and exclude the variance from an effect I don't care about?
messages.subject_clean: can I make posterior predictions in rstanarm and exclude the variance from an effect I don't care about?
messages.body_plain:
I'm doing a meta-analysis and I've got a model in which I include a study-level effect:

m = stan_glmer(y ~ 1 + x + (1|studyid), data=data)

At prediction time, I want to make population level predictions, excluding this extra source of study-level variance. I could setup a prediction dataset with studyid = "_NEW_studyid" but I don't think that's right--instead of a population level prediction I believe that this gives me a prediction for what I'd find in a new study. (Meaning the means should be the same as what I want, but with wider credible intervals...?)

I can of course generate any posterior quantity I want using the draws, I just wanted to know whether I was missing some simple way to get what I wanted without doing that.
Seth

On Wednesday, July 27, 2016 at 6:52:11 AM UTC-4, Seth Flaxman wrote:
> I'm doing a meta-analysis and I've got a model in which I include a study-level effect:
>
> m = stan_glmer(y ~ 1 + x + (1|studyid), data=data)
>
> At prediction time, I want to make population level predictions, excluding this extra source of study-level variance. I could setup a prediction dataset with studyid = "_NEW_studyid" but I don't think that's right--instead of a population level prediction I believe that this gives me a prediction for what I'd find in a new study. (Meaning the means should be the same as what I want, but with wider credible intervals...?)

If the studyid variable contains _any_ level that was not among the levels that were used when the model was estimated, then it grabs the _NEW_studyid shift in the intercept for that level when doing posterior_predict(). You don't have to name the new level _NEW_.

Ben

I have a model that reaches large tree-depths during warmup (up to 17)

expected tree-depth during sampling, but below the maximally reached
tree-depth during warmup (say 14). I would basically set the max-
treedepth to a value that results in some but not too many max-treedepth
iterations during warmup.

I understand Michael Betancourt's response  <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/hjYWqJZfSgw/fQIKJanxcWoJ>in another thread so that

saturates at the maximum during sampling. That is, it should not be a
problem if max-treedepth is reached a few times during warmup.

Does this sound like a reasonable approach?
Or does hitting max tree-depth in during warmup disturb the adaptation
of sampler parameters?

Best - Guido

interest that's derived from the posterior; I don't think I'm doing
anything weird here. But I can see why it's not at all easy to make
this automatic.

zeros out the draws for the parameter I don't care about (feedback
welcome):

 i = grep("^b\\[",rownames(model$stan_summary))[1]
 j = which(rownames(model$stan_summary) == "b[(Intercept)
studyid:_NEW_studyid]")

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] max tree-depth in warmup and sampling
messages.body_plain:
High treedepth in warmup but reasonable treedepth in sampling
is caused by a small step size in warmup which is caused by
parameters with very different posterior variances.  Just scan
through the diagonal elements of the mass matrix to find any
extremely high or small values (the values are just the marginal
posterior variances, or approximations there of) and target
the corresponding parameters for rescaling (note that the mass
matrix elements correspond to parameters in the unconstrained
space, in case you have any constraints).

For example, if mu and sigma are the marginal posterior mean
and variance of the parameter x then the model

parameters {
  real x;
}

model {
  x ~ blah;
}

would be easier to adapt with the modification

transformed data {
  real mu;
  real sigma;
  mu = …;
  sigma = …;
}

parameters {
  real x_tilde;
}

model {
  mu + sigma * x_tilde ~ blah; // no jacobian needed for linear transform
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: can I make posterior predictions in rstanarm and exclude the variance from an effect I don't care about?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: can I make posterior predictions in rstanarm and exclude the variance from an effect I don't care about?
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, July 28, 2016 at 6:41:10 AM UTC-4, Seth Flaxman wrote:
> I guess you're making a semantic distinction in terms of what a
> "posterior prediction" is? What I'm trying to predict is a quantity of
> interest that's derived from the posterior; I don't think I'm doing
> anything weird here. But I can see why it's not at all easy to make
> this automatic.

Those predictions aren't posterior. If the new observation came from an old grouping level, you would integrate over its intercept shift to come up with a predictive distribution that is consistent with Bayes Rule. If the new observation came from a new grouping level, you would integrate over the prior distribution of intercept shifts using the posterior distribution of the group-level variance to come up with a predictive distribution that is consistent with Bayes Rule. But if you fix the intercept shift to be zero rather than integrating over it, then the predictions are not consistent with Bayes Rule.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
No, there is a dangerous trade off there.  If you cap the max treedepth
then you can get drastically fewer effective samples in each adaptation
window, which would lead to _noisier_ mass matrix estimation and
_even worse trajectories in the next window_.

The problem is that in order to speed things up you have to very
delicately tune the adaptation parameters, such as the various window sizes,
in order to get just enough effective samples to get a reasonably convergent
series of mass matrix estimates.  There’s no general solution to this, and
I certainly don’t feel comfortable relying on it myself.

I think it’s much easier to focus on the latent cause, which is the huge
variation in marginal variances.  Having parameters on similar scales
usually leads to more interpretable models, anyways, and so may
indicate a somewhat ill-posed model.

messages.subject: Mapping Latent States to Data with Gaussian Processes
messages.subject_clean: Mapping Latent States to Data with Gaussian Processes
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to implement a model by Neil Lawrence called "Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model (GP-LVM)". Link to paper here. <http://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume6/lawrence05a/lawrence05a.pdf> The gist of it is that we have N D-dimensional observations that we call Y, and we assume that these N observations each have a lower dimensional representation as a Q-dimensional vector. We call the latent representation of these vectors together, X.  They are related by y_d | X ~ MultivariateNormal(0, K(X)) where y_d is the dth column of our data Y and K(X) is a covariance function of our latent states that allows us to model non-linear relations between the data and latent states (Gaussian Process). I should also mention that X itself has a multivariate normal prior that's isotropic.

So the main unknown parameters we are trying to estimate here is the NxQ matrix X, and the (hyper)parameters of the Gaussian Kernel. In the paper Lawrence just uses MAP estimation, and I believe in subsequent papers he starts using variational inference, but I personally would like to use MCMC for various reasons. I'm attaching the code for the Stan model a wrote up along with some synthetic data I made, as an R object. I ran as follows:

synth_dat <- list(
  N = 100,
  D = 10,
  Q = 2,
  Y = s$Y
)

fit <- stan(file = 'acit_gplvm.stan', data = synth_dat,
            iter = 100, chains = 1)

which took about an hour on my laptop. The posteriors (of X at least) seem to reasonably capture the true X's, so I'm tempted to say things are working.

One thing I'm wondering is if anyone sees any immediate ways I can speed this up (vectorization). Also I feel like this model is prone to the funnel problem. I'd imagine that if certain scales, inv_l, are high this affects the X's a lot. I'm also worried about scaling, I eventually need to get N=1000, but that means that at every leapfrog step Stan has to compute 1000 entries of that matrix, then do the Cholesky routine for the multivariate likelihood, and that's not even accounting for computing gradients. Does thing stand a chance of working with MCMC or will I have to resort to variational methods?

On Thu, Jul 28, 2016 at 4:55 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> On Thursday, July 28, 2016 at 6:41:10 AM UTC-4, Seth Flaxman wrote:
>>
>> I guess you're making a semantic distinction in terms of what a
>> "posterior prediction" is? What I'm trying to predict is a quantity of
>> interest that's derived from the posterior; I don't think I'm doing
>> anything weird here. But I can see why it's not at all easy to make
>> this automatic.
>
>
> Those predictions aren't posterior. If the new observation came from an old
> grouping level, you would integrate over its intercept shift to come up with
> a predictive distribution that is consistent with Bayes Rule. If the new
> observation came from a new grouping level, you would integrate over the
> prior distribution of intercept shifts using the posterior distribution of
> the group-level variance to come up with a predictive distribution that is
> consistent with Bayes Rule. But if you fix the intercept shift to be zero
> rather than integrating over it, then the predictions are not consistent
> with Bayes Rule.
>
> Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Advice on optimizing Stan code: Nested mixed logit
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Advice on optimizing Stan code: Nested mixed logit
messages.body_plain:
First off, 2.10 introduced a bug which we have already
patched.  So hopefully you're using 2.9 or earlier or already
have 2.11.

You can't diagnose convergence with one chain---you want to use at
least two and preferably four.

In terms of n_eff, the non-centered parameterization is the
best thing to try.

But you also have an extra degree of freedom, so the model's
not strictly identifiable in the likelihood, so the priors are
driving convergence.  There's a discussion in the manual regression
chapter under heading "identifiability" (p. 60 for v2.10).

You also want to make the arithmetic more robust.  Basically,
avoid use of exp() which can overflow and underflow easily.  See below.

> On Jul 28, 2016, at 10:41 PM, al hanz seiji lidasan <hanzl...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi, we are currently testing the application of Stan for discrete choice models for mode choice in transportation using simple simulated data.
> Specifically, the model we are testing is nested mixed logit with 3 choices namely, "car", "rail", "bus" with rail and bus correlated in one nest due to their public transit nature and car in another nest.
> The correlation is modeled as error terms (eps) that comes from a single distribution N(0,sigma).
> We were able to recover the results of the toy model by comparing the Stan model to a maximum-likelihood estimate.
> However, we are concerned regarding the very low effective number of samples.
> Is there a way to improve the estimate of the effective number of samples?
> I have attached our Stan code and the simulated data so it can be replicated.
> The Stan code, result of the Stan code and the maximum likelihood estimate are shown below.
>
>
> data <- read.csv(file="35.csv",header=T)
> ns <- nrow(data); n.alt <- 3; n.var <- 1
>
> mnl_code <-  "
> data {
>     int<lower=2> K;  //number of alternatives
>     int<lower=0> N;  //number of samples
>     int<lower=1> D;  //number of variables
>     int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N,K];  //outcome for each sample
>     matrix [K,D]  x[N];  //matrix of variables
> }
>
> parameters {
>     vector[D] beta;
>     real<lower=0> sigma;  //hypersigma
>     vector[N] eps; //error terms
> }
>
> //transformed parameters {
> //}
>
> model {
>     beta ~normal(0,10);
>     eps ~ normal(0,sigma);
>     sigma ~ normal(0,1);
>     for (n in 1:N) {
>            vector[K] v; vector[K] lp;
>                v = x[n]*beta;
>                   lp[1] = log( exp(v[1]        )/( exp(v[1])+exp(v[2]+eps[n])+exp(v[3]+eps[n])) );
>                   lp[2] = log( exp(v[2]+eps[n] )/( exp(v[1])+exp(v[2]+eps[n])+exp(v[3]+eps[n])) );
>                   lp[3] = log( exp(v[3]+eps[n] )/( exp(v[1])+exp(v[2]+eps[n])+exp(v[3]+eps[n])) );
>                   target += lp[1]*y[n,1]+lp[2]*y[n,2]+lp[3]*y[n,3];

I take it the eps is the effect of public transportation?

You can use matrix multiply for x * beta:

  vector[K] v;
  v = x * beta;

You should gather and share all subterms rather than reapplying exp(), etc.

We have a built-in function to do all of this:

  vector[3] zz;

  zz[1] = v[n, 1];
  zz[2] = v[n, 2] + eps[n];
  zz[3] = v[n, 3] + eps[n];
  target += y[n] * log(softmax(zz));

That should also be a bit more stable arithmetically.

This is where the extra degree of freedom is.  You can add
any constant to v and get the same answer.  Then if
you pin v[n,1] = 0, you get the same problem in that
you can't identify v and eps because you can add to one
and subtract from the other.

- Bob

If you're trying to match, that mean = 5 will get absorbed
into the intercept.

In terms of fitting efficiency in Stan, it helps to standardize
so that the slope and intercept are on the unit scale (roughly
1 sd).  Otherwise, Stan has to do the adaptation during warmup,
which should still work, but might require smaller initial step
sizes and longer warmup periods.

messages.body_plain:
You have some marginal variances on the order of 1e-4, and some of
the order 1.  Without the proper mass matrix HMC will typical require a
step size sqrt(1e-4 / 1) = 1e-2 times smaller, hence 100 times longer
trajectories.  This can lead to slow adaptation, especially if your model
is already difficult to sample.

You can always arbitrarily rescale your parameters, as I tried to explain
before.  If you know the parameter x has posterior mean mu and
posterior standard deviation sigma, say from a previous run, then
rewrite your model as

parameters {
  real x_tilde;
}
transformed parameters {
  real x;
  x = mu + sigma * x_tilde;
}
model {
  // use x
}

By construct x_tilde will have unit marginal variance and hence admit
a much easier adaptation.

messages.body_plain:
The notion of "convergence" for warmup is that all the
chains find the same mass matrix and step size.

There are several obstacles to this, though.  First is
that you need to get to the typical set (where the posterior
mass is and where you find truly random draws from the posterior)
and you then need to spend enough time there to get a good
estimate of the mass matrix.  This is made more difficult (in
a good diagnostic way) by starting with diffuse initializations
and the general random nature of MCMC (and hence our adaptation,
which is very much like MCMC even though it's not properly
Markovian).  Another big obstacle is varying posterior curvature
(i.e., models where the matrix of second derivatives of the log
density w.r.t. the parameters varies around the posterior);  then
there isn't a good global mass matrix.

I believe there is a lot of room for improvement in adaptation using
parallelization and second derivative calculations.  We're looking
for a grad student or postdoc to help us investigate.  Hint hint.

- Bob

On Sun, Jul 31, 2016 at 5:30 PM Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> The notion of "convergence" for warmup is that all the
> chains find the same mass matrix and step size.
>
> There are several obstacles to this, though.  First is
> that you need to get to the typical set (where the posterior
> mass is and where you find truly random draws from the posterior)
> and you then need to spend enough time there to get a good
> estimate of the mass matrix.  This is made more difficult (in
> a good diagnostic way) by starting with diffuse initializations
> and the general random nature of MCMC (and hence our adaptation,
> which is very much like MCMC even though it's not properly
> Markovian).  Another big obstacle is varying posterior curvature
> (i.e., models where the matrix of second derivatives of the log
> density w.r.t. the parameters varies around the posterior);  then
> there isn't a good global mass matrix.
>
> I believe there is a lot of room for improvement in adaptation using
> parallelization and second derivative calculations.  We're looking
> for a grad student or postdoc to help us investigate.  Hint hint.
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
We're working on making some of these operations more efficient,
like the squared exponential covariance function, but the
real bottleneck is here:

 for(d in 1:D)
    Y[,d] ~ multi_normal(mu, K[d]);

That's where we have to solve a matrix.

If you make inv_l a matrix, you can use to_vector()
to vectorize, but this isn't much of a bottleneck.

I'm not a GP expert by any means, so I don't have any comment
on the model.

You could use the non-centered parameterization here:

 for (n in 1:N)
    to_vector(X[n]) ~ normal(0, sigma_sq_x);

by taking

  to_vector(X_raw[n]) ~ normal(0, 1);

  X = sigma_sq_x * X_raw;

Stan uses scale (sigma) rather than variance (sigma^2)
parameterization of normal (but variance param of multi-normal).

- Bob

> On Jul 28, 2016, at 4:52 PM, Arya Pourzanjani <ar...@umail.ucsb.edu> wrote:
>
> I'm trying to implement a model by Neil Lawrence called "Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model (GP-LVM)". Link to paper here. The gist of it is that we have N D-dimensional observations that we call Y, and we assume that these N observations each have a lower dimensional representation as a Q-dimensional vector. We call the latent representation of these vectors together, X.  They are related by y_d | X ~ MultivariateNormal(0, K(X)) where y_d is the dth column of our data Y and K(X) is a covariance function of our latent states that allows us to model non-linear relations between the data and latent states (Gaussian Process). I should also mention that X itself has a multivariate normal prior that's isotropic.
>
> So the main unknown parameters we are trying to estimate here is the NxQ matrix X, and the (hyper)parameters of the Gaussian Kernel. In the paper Lawrence just uses MAP estimation, and I believe in subsequent papers he starts using variational inference, but I personally would like to use MCMC for various reasons. I'm attaching the code for the Stan model a wrote up along with some synthetic data I made, as an R object. I ran as follows:
>
> synth_dat <- list(
>   N = 100,
>   D = 10,
>   Q = 2,
>   Y = s$Y
> )
>
> fit <- stan(file = 'acit_gplvm.stan', data = synth_dat,
>             iter = 100, chains = 1)
>
> which took about an hour on my laptop. The posteriors (of X at least) seem to reasonably capture the true X's, so I'm tempted to say things are working.
>
> One thing I'm wondering is if anyone sees any immediate ways I can speed this up (vectorization). Also I feel like this model is prone to the funnel problem. I'd imagine that if certain scales, inv_l, are high this affects the X's a lot. I'm also worried about scaling, I eventually need to get N=1000, but that means that at every leapfrog step Stan has to compute 1000 entries of that matrix, then do the Cholesky routine for the multivariate likelihood, and that's not even accounting for computing gradients. Does thing stand a chance of working with MCMC or will I have to resort to variational methods?
>
